3124:        "text": "     1\t**chevron::process::****WindowEnvelope**\n     2\t\n     3\t*Class Design Description*\n     4\t\n     5\t# What WindowEnvelope Is\n     6\t\n     7\tWindowEnvelope is the **per-window infrastructure**** (PWI)**** container** that represents a single live window within Chevron\u2019s runtime. It bundles the raw backend window handle produced by a user-supplied factory with the identity, lifecycle machinery, and per-window infrastructure that Chevron provides unconditionally for every window it governs.\n     8\t\n     9\tIt is not the framework window itself. It is the structure that surrounds that window \u2014 giving it a stable identity within Chevron, a home for its infrastructure, and a handle through which every upstream class in the system can reason about it uniformly regardless of what GUI framework is underneath.\n    10\t\n    11\tIt is not inheritable. Extensibility is provided through WindowComponentStore, the typed component container the envelope owns. User code never subclasses WindowEnvelope, it extends what lives inside it.\n    12\t\n    13\tIt is not:\n    14\t\n    15\t- The backend window object or a wrapper around its API\n    16\t\n    17\t- A window manager or event router\n    18\t\n    19\t- Directly user-constructible\n    20\t\n    21\t- A base class for user-defined window types\n    22\t\n    23\t# Where WindowEnvelope Sits in the Layering Model\n    24\t\n    25\tWindowEnvelope occupies the innermost named layer of Chevron\u2019s lifetime hierarchy. Every instance is produced by WindowDispatcher via a factory call and immediately transferred to WindowCoordinator, which owns it for the remainder of its lifetime. The envelope exists only while the GUI engine is active.\n    26\t\n    27\tProcess lifetime   ->   AppProcess\n    28\t\n    29\tGUI lifetime       ->   GUIEngine\n    30\t\n    31\t                          |- WindowDispatcher    (creation authority)\n    32\t\n    33\t                          |- WindowCoordinator   (lifetime authority)\n    34\t\n    35\t                          |    |- WindowHierarchy (relationship graph)\n    36\t\n    37\tWindow lifetime    ->   WindowEnvelope\n    38\t\n    39\t                          |- WindowComponentStore (PWI components)\n    40\t\n    41\tThe envelope is the unit of currency in Chevron\u2019s window layer. Every operation that WindowCoordinator performs \u2014 tracking, querying, teardown ordering \u2014 is performed on envelopes. Every operation that GUIEngine orchestrates \u2014 subsidiary window parenting, shutdown sequencing, lifecycle event propagation \u2014 is performed through envelopes. The uniform handle the envelope provides is what allows upstream classes to reason about any window without knowing anything about the underlying framework.\n    42\t\n    43\t# What Problem WindowEnvelope Is Solving\n    44\t\n    45\tWithout a uniform per-window container, Chevron has no clean way to associate its own infrastructure with a live window. The framework window handle is a raw pointer with no Chevron semantics attached. The coordinator can track it by address, but it cannot ask it for a logging context, a memory arena, or a view system, these things have nowhere to reside.\n    46\t\n    47\tWindowEnvelope solves this by being the place those things live. It gives every window a stable Chevron identity and a structured home for per-window infrastructure. Because the envelope is always present and always uniformly structured, any Chevron subsystem can reach into any live window\u2019s envelope and reliably find the components it needs \u2014 without knowing anything about the specific window, its factory, or the framework behind it.\n    48\t\n    49\tThis is the mechanism by which per-window infrastructure becomes a first-class library feature rather than something each application has to wire up manually.\n    50\t\n    51\t# Core Responsibilities (Non-Negotiable)\n    52\t\n    53\tWindowEnvelope has exactly four responsibilities:\n    54\t\n    55\t- Hold the raw backend window handle for the duration of the window\u2019s lifetime\n    56\t\n    57\t- Carry the identity information Chevron assigns\n    58\t\n    59\t- Maintain a WindowComponentStore\n    60\t\n    61\t- Expose a lifecycle hook surface that Chevron\u2019s internal infrastructure can bind into\n    62\t\n    63\t*The envelope is a structured container with a governed lifetime, not a service or a policy class.*\n    64\t\n    65\t# What WindowEnvelope Carries\n    66\t\n    67\t## The Backend Window Handle\n    68\t\n    69\tThe raw handle to the framework window \u2014 a wxFrame*, a QMainWindow*, or equivalent \u2014 produced by the user\u2019s factory callable. This is the one genuinely framework-specific piece inside an otherwise framework-agnostic structure. It is required and always present. Its lifetime is governed by the envelope: Chevron owns the handle from the moment the envelope is constructed and is responsible for its destruction during teardown.\n    70\t\n    71\t## Identity\n    72\t\n    73\tThe envelope carries three stable identity values, all set at construction and immutable for the envelope\u2019s lifetime:\n    74\t\n    75\t- **Instance ID: **A unique sequential identifier assigned by WindowCoordinator at the moment it takes ownership of the envelope. This is the envelope\u2019s identity within Chevron, the handle by which upstream classes target operations against this specific live window.\n    76\t\n    77\t- **Factory ID: **The identifier of the WindowFactory that produced this envelope, embedded at dispatch time. This identifies the kind of window this envelope represents and is used by WindowCoordinator for single-instance queries and by-factory filtering.\n    78\t\n    79\t- **Window kind: **A WindowKind enumeration value \u2014 either top-level or subsidiary \u2014 set at dispatch time based on how the factory was dispatched. This is structural information, not a runtime state. A top-level window is a regular window. A subsidiary window was dispatched with a declared parent and its backend window was constructed with that parent relationship made real through the framework.\n    80\t\n    81\t## WindowComponentStore\n    82\t\n    83\tThe envelope owns a WindowComponentStore \u2014 a component container that holds all per-window infrastructure associated with this window instance. Each component is a distinct named type. Components are stored under std::type_index keys and retrieved by type, with no shared base class required.\n    84\t\n    85\tChevron populates a set of **base components** unconditionally at construction time for every envelope. These are the pieces of per-window infrastructure that Chevron provides as a matter of course \u2014 things like a memory arena scoped to window lifetime, a logging context tagged to this window, a component messaging client, and dynamic view infrastructure. The precise base component set is defined by the PWI design phase and is deferred, but the pattern is fixed: base components are always present and their population is guaranteed by the construction pathway.\n    86\t\n    87\tBeyond the base set, both Chevron subsystems and user code may register **optional components** at any point during the envelope\u2019s lifetime. Optional components follow the same type-keyed storage model. Each type may only be registered once per envelope \u2014 a duplicate registration is a caught error. The store is internally synchronized with a mutex, making it safe for optional component registration to occur from any thread without the caller needing to coordinate access.\n    88\t\n    89\tFor windows where even the base component set is unnecessary overhead \u2014 transient dialogs, splash screens, lightweight utility windows \u2014 the **lightweight flag** on the WindowFactory descriptor signals that only the minimum viable infrastructure should be initialized. What \u201cminimum viable\u201d means precisely is a deferred PWI decision, but the mechanism for requesting it is settled at the descriptor level.\n    90\t\n    91\t# Construction Pathway\n    92\t\n    93\tUser code does not construct WindowEnvelope directly. The constructor is not part of the public interface. Instead, Chevron provides a controlled construction function that is the only legitimate way to produce an envelope instance.\n    94\t\n    95\tInside a factory callable, the flow is:\n    96\t\n    97\t- The user code factory call receives a WindowInitContext assembled by Chevron at dispatch time\n    98\t\n    99\t- The factory constructs the backend window instance using information from the WindowInitContext as needed \u2014 including the parent window handle for subsidiary windows\n   100\t\n   101\t- The factory passes the backend window handle and the WindowInitContext to the Chevron defined envelope constructor method\n   102\t\n   103\t- Chevron constructs the envelope internally, assigns identity, populates base components, and returns a std::unique_ptr<WindowEnvelope>\n   104\t\n   105\t- The user code factory returns that pointer, transferring ownership to WindowDispatcher, which immediately hands it to WindowCoordinator\n   106\t\n   107\tThis pathway ensures that no WindowEnvelope can exist without a valid WindowInitContext having been involved in its construction. The WindowInitContext is the authority token that makes the construction legitimate. Without it, there is no envelope.\n   108\t\n   109\t# What WindowEnvelope Deliberately Does Not Own\n   110\t\n   111\t*This boundary is just as important as what it does own.*\n   112\t\n   113\tWindowEnvelope does not own:\n   114\t\n   115\t- Window state visible to the framework.\n   116\t\n   117\t- Relationship data.\n   118\t\n   119\t- Its own lifetime \u2014 that belongs to WindowCoordinator.\n   120\t\n   121\t- Knowledge of other live envelopes or the state of the application\u2019s window population.\n   122\t\n   123\t- Any framework-specific API surface beyond holding the raw handle.\n   124\t\n   125\t# Lifetime of WindowEnvelope\n   126\t\n   127\tAn envelope is born when WindowDispatcher fires a factory and transfers the result to WindowCoordinator. It lives for as long as WindowCoordinator holds it in its registry. It is destroyed when the coordinator winds it down, either as part of the shutdown sequence or in response to the underlying framework window being closed.\n   128\t\n   129\tDuring teardown, the envelope\u2019s components are destroyed in the reverse order of their registration. 3137:      "json_block": "{\"language\": \"plaintext\", \"code\": \"**chevron::process::****WindowEnvelope**\\n\\n*Class Design Description*\\n\\n# What WindowEnvelope Is\\n\\nWindowEnvelope is the **per-window infrastructure**** (PWI)**** container** that represents a single live window within Chevron\\u2019s runtime. It bundles the raw backend window handle produced by a user-supplied factory with the identity, lifecycle machinery, and per-window infrastructure that Chevron provides unconditionally for every window it governs.\\n\\nIt is not the framework window itself. It is the structure that surrounds that window \\u2014 giving it a stable identity within Chevron, a home for its infrastructure, and a handle through which every upstream class in the system can reason about it uniformly regardless of what GUI framework is underneath.\\n\\nIt is not inheritable. Extensibility is provided through WindowComponentStore, the typed component container the envelope owns. User code never subclasses WindowEnvelope, it extends what lives inside it.\\n\\nIt is not:\\n\\n- The backend window object or a wrapper around its API\\n\\n- A window manager or event router\\n\\n- Directly user-constructible\\n\\n- A base class for user-defined window types\\n\\n# Where WindowEnvelope Sits in the Layering Model\\n\\nWindowEnvelope occupies the innermost named layer of Chevron\\u2019s lifetime hierarchy. Every instance is produced by WindowDispatcher via a factory call and immediately transferred to WindowCoordinator, which owns it for the remainder of its lifetime. The envelope exists only while the GUI engine is active.\\n\\nProcess lifetime   ->   AppProcess\\n\\nGUI lifetime       ->   GUIEngine\\n\\n                          |- WindowDispatcher    (creation authority)\\n\\n                          |- WindowCoordinator   (lifetime authority)\\n\\n                          |    |- WindowHierarchy (relationship graph)\\n\\nWindow lifetime    ->   WindowEnvelope\\n\\n                          |- WindowComponentStore (PWI components)\\n\\nThe envelope is the unit of currency in Chevron\\u2019s window layer. Every operation that WindowCoordinator performs \\u2014 tracking, querying, teardown ordering \\u2014 is performed on envelopes. Every operation that GUIEngine orchestrates \\u2014 subsidiary window parenting, shutdown sequencing, lifecycle event propagation \\u2014 is performed through envelopes. The uniform handle the envelope provides is what allows upstream classes to reason about any window without knowing anything about the underlying framework.\\n\\n# What Problem WindowEnvelope Is Solving\\n\\nWithout a uniform per-window container, Chevron has no clean way to associate its own infrastructure with a live window. The framework window handle is a raw pointer with no Chevron semantics attached. The coordinator can track it by address, but it cannot ask it for a logging context, a memory arena, or a view system, these things have nowhere to reside.\\n\\nWindowEnvelope solves this by being the place those things live. It gives every window a stable Chevron identity and a structured home for per-window infrastructure. Because the envelope is always present and always uniformly structured, any Chevron subsystem can reach into any live window\\u2019s envelope and reliably find the components it needs \\u2014 without knowing anything about the specific window, its factory, or the framework behind it.\\n\\nThis is the mechanism by which per-window infrastructure becomes a first-class library feature rather than something each application has to wire up manually.\\n\\n# Core Responsibilities (Non-Negotiable)\\n\\nWindowEnvelope has exactly four responsibilities:\\n\\n- Hold the raw backend window handle for the duration of the window\\u2019s lifetime\\n\\n- Carry the identity information Chevron assigns\\n\\n- Maintain a WindowComponentStore\\n\\n- Expose a lifecycle hook surface that Chevron\\u2019s internal infrastructure can bind into\\n\\n*The envelope is a structured container with a governed lifetime, not a service or a policy class.*\\n\\n# What WindowEnvelope Carries\\n\\n## The Backend Window Handle\\n\\nThe raw handle to the framework window \\u2014 a wxFrame*, a QMainWindow*, or equivalent \\u2014 produced by the user\\u2019s factory callable. This is the one genuinely framework-specific piece inside an otherwise framework-agnostic structure. It is required and always present. Its lifetime is governed by the envelope: Chevron owns the handle from the moment the envelope is constructed and is responsible for its destruction during teardown.\\n\\n## Identity\\n\\nThe envelope carries three stable identity values, all set at construction and immutable for the envelope\\u2019s lifetime:\\n\\n- **Instance ID: **A unique sequential identifier assigned by WindowCoordinator at the moment it takes ownership of the envelope. This is the envelope\\u2019s identity within Chevron, the handle by which upstream classes target operations against this specific live window.\\n\\n- **Factory ID: **The identifier of the WindowFactory that produced this envelope, embedded at dispatch time. This identifies the kind of window this envelope represents and is used by WindowCoordinator for single-instance queries and by-factory filtering.\\n\\n- **Window kind: **A WindowKind enumeration value \\u2014 either top-level or subsidiary \\u2014 set at dispatch time based on how the factory was dispatched. This is structural information, not a runtime state. A top-level window is a regular window. A subsidiary window was dispatched with a declared parent and its backend window was constructed with that parent relationship made real through the framework.\\n\\n## WindowComponentStore\\n\\nThe envelope owns a WindowComponentStore \\u2014 a component container that holds all per-window infrastructure associated with this window instance. Each component is a distinct named type. Components are stored under std::type_index keys and retrieved by type, with no shared base class required.\\n\\nChevron populates a set of **base components** unconditionally at construction time for every envelope. These are the pieces of per-window infrastructure that Chevron provides as a matter of course \\u2014 things like a memory arena scoped to window lifetime, a logging context tagged to this window, a component messaging client, and dynamic view infrastructure. The precise base component set is defined by the PWI design phase and is deferred, but the pattern is fixed: base components are always present and their population is guaranteed by the construction pathway.\\n\\nBeyond the base set, both Chevron subsystems and user code may register **optional components** at any point during the envelope\\u2019s lifetime. Optional components follow the same type-keyed storage model. Each type may only be registered once per envelope \\u2014 a duplicate registration is a caught error. The store is internally synchronized with a mutex, making it safe for optional component registration to occur from any thread without the caller needing to coordinate access.\\n\\nFor windows where even the base component set is unnecessary overhead \\u2014 transient dialogs, splash screens, lightweight utility windows \\u2014 the **lightweight flag** on the WindowFactory descriptor signals that only the minimum viable infrastructure should be initialized. What \\u201cminimum viable\\u201d means precisely is a deferred PWI decision, but the mechanism for requesting it is settled at the descriptor level.\\n\\n# Construction Pathway\\n\\nUser code does not construct WindowEnvelope directly. The constructor is not part of the public interface. Instead, Chevron provides a controlled construction function that is the only legitimate way to produce an envelope instance.\\n\\nInside a factory callable, the flow is:\\n\\n- The user code factory call receives a WindowInitContext assembled by Chevron at dispatch time\\n\\n- The factory constructs the backend window instance using information from the WindowInitContext as needed \\u2014 including the parent window handle for subsidiary windows\\n\\n- The factory passes the backend window handle and the WindowInitContext to the Chevron defined envelope constructor method\\n\\n- Chevron constructs the envelope internally, assigns identity, populates base components, and returns a std::unique_ptr<WindowEnvelope>\\n\\n- The user code factory returns that pointer, transferring ownership to WindowDispatcher, which immediately hands it to WindowCoordinator\\n\\nThis pathway ensures that no WindowEnvelope can exist without a valid WindowInitContext having been involved in its construction. The WindowInitContext is the authority token that makes the construction legitimate. Without it, there is no envelope.\\n\\n# What WindowEnvelope Deliberately Does Not Own\\n\\n*This boundary is just as important as what it does own.*\\n\\nWindowEnvelope does not own:\\n\\n- Window state visible to the framework.\\n\\n- Relationship data.\\n\\n- Its own lifetime \\u2014 that belongs to WindowCoordinator.\\n\\n- Knowledge of other live envelopes or the state of the application\\u2019s window population.\\n\\n- Any framework-specific API surface beyond holding the raw handle.\\n\\n# Lifetime of WindowEnvelope\\n\\nAn envelope is born when WindowDispatcher fires a factory and transfers the result to WindowCoordinator. It lives for as long as WindowCoordinator holds it in its registry. It is destroyed when the coordinator winds it down, either as part of the shutdown sequence or in response to the underlying framework window being closed.\\n\\nDuring teardown, the envelope\\u2019s components are destroyed in the reverse order of their registration. The backend window handle is released last. At the end of teardown, the envelope is removed from the coordinator\\u2019s registry and destroyed. Nothing may reference it after that point.\\n\\n*An envelope\\u2019s lifetime is the window\\u2019s lifetime from Chevron\\u2019s perspective. When the envelope is gone, the window is gone.*\\n\\n# Error Handling Philosophy\\n\\nWindowEnvelope and its construction pathway should:\\n\\n- Treat any attempt to construct an envelope outside of Chevron\\u2019s control as a hard error\\n\\n- Guarantee that base components are fully populated before the envelope is returned from construction\\n\\n- Catch duplicate component registrations immediately and surface them as errors\\n\\n- Fail fast on any attempt to access the component store after the envelope has begun teardown\\n\\n**Note: **The boundary between returned error codes and thrown exceptions follows the same open question as the rest of the library \\u2014 deferred pending library-wide error handling strategy decisions.\\n\\n# Open Questions and Deferred Decisions\\n\\nThe following are known open questions that are intentionally deferred:\\n\\n- **Base component set: **The precise set of components Chevron populates unconditionally in every envelope \\u2014 which subsystems qualify, what they are named, and in what order they are initialized \\u2014 is deferred to dedicated PWI design work. I agree and acknowledge that the relationship between 'WindowDispatcher' and 'WindowCoordinator' will have to be handled with a well designed mechanism to make that relationship clear in the code. We will certainly want to think about how that might work in general, maybe dependency injection? But as you said, this is for later as our focus lies elsewhere right now. It is also expected that a concrete implementation of a 'GUIEngine' won't be trivial. I also want to ask, are you under the impression that the\u00a0'WindowDispatcher' and 'WindowCoordinator' classes live as actual instances at the base interface level, or as independently constructed by every implementation at their level? I was thinking the whole window management situation would be handled in a more GUI agnostic manner (so at the base class level, but I am open to suggestions) to help cut down on the amount of work that needs to be done per implementation. That's kind of where the \"window envelope\" idea came from. Well, that and being able to attach \"per window\" infrastructure behind the windows.\u00a0Think of it like a struct of \"things Chevron needs per window\":\n\n1. The backend window (required)\n* `wxFrame*`, etc.\n* Created by the GUI runtime\n* Owned and destroyed by Chevron\n\n2. Per-window infrastructure (this is the big one)\nThis is where the library actually becomes valuable.\nExamples:\n* Logging context (tagged to window)\n* Memory arenas scoped to window lifetime\n* Event bridges\n* Viewport / Page system\n* Layout-independent navigation state\nThis is Chevron's playground.\n\n3. Internal identity\n* Window key\n* Runtime ID\n* Maybe hierarchy info later\n\n4. Lifecycle hooks (internal)\n* On create\n* On destroy\n* Maybe event binding glue\n\nThese are just rough ideas but coming close to what I am looking for. 2693:    "text": " This is the right call. `WindowEnvelope` sits exactly at that boundary \u2014 we need to describe it well enough that its role and structure are clear, while being honest that the specifics of what lives inside it are deliberately deferred to a future design phase. Let me compile everything we've established so far and make sure we're aligned before writing anything.\n\n---\n\n**What we know the envelope is:**\n\nIt is the per-window container that bundles everything Chevron needs for a single live window instance. It is not the framework window itself \u2014 it wraps the raw backend window handle and surrounds it with Chevron's own per-window infrastructure. Its lifetime is governed entirely by `WindowCoordinator`. It only exists while the GUI engine is active.\n\n---\n\n**What the envelope carries \u2014 settled:**\n\nThe raw backend window handle \u2014 the `wxFrame*`, `QMainWindow*`, or equivalent. This is required and always present. It is the one piece that is genuinely framework-specific inside an otherwise framework-agnostic structure.\n\nIts own unique instance ID, assigned by `WindowCoordinator` at receipt time.\n\nThe factory ID of the `WindowFactory` that produced it, embedded at dispatch time.\n\nIts `WindowKind` \u2014 an enum distinguishing a regular top-level window from a subsidiary window. This is set at construction and does not change.\n\nThe typed attachment container \u2014 a type-keyed map that holds both Chevron's unconditional base attachments and any optional user-defined attachments. This is the PWI mechanism.\n\n---\n\n**What the envelope carries \u2014 the attachment model:**\n\nChevron populates a set of base attachments unconditionally at construction time for every envelope. These are the things that make sense for essentially all windows \u2014 a memory arena scoped to window lifetime, some form of dynamic view/viewport mechanism, logging context tagged to this window, lifecycle hook bindings, and whatever else the PWI design eventually prescribes. The precise list is deferred but the pattern is settled: they go in as typed attachments through the same mechanism user code uses, they're just always there.\n\nUser code can add their own typed attachments through a defined registration pathway. The retrieval interface is type-keyed \u2014 you ask the envelope for the attachment of type T and get it or get nothing. No string keys, no integers, just types as identities. Attachments don't share a common base type.\n\nThe envelope controls what can be attached and when. Chevron's base attachments are populated during construction via `WindowInitContext`. The user attachment registration pathway is a deferred design question \u2014 we know it needs to exist, we don't know its exact shape yet.\n\n---\n\n**What the envelope does not own:**\n\nWindow state visible to the framework \u2014 focus, z-order, visibility. The framework owns that. Relationship data \u2014 no parent or child references live on the envelope. That's `WindowHierarchy`'s concern. Its own lifetime \u2014 that belongs to `WindowCoordinator`.\n\n---\n\n**Construction:**\n\nThe envelope is produced by a factory callable. The factory accepts a single `WindowInitContext` and returns a `std::unique_ptr<WindowEnvelope>`. The `WindowInitContext` carries everything needed to bootstrap Chevron's base attachments unconditionally, plus optional parent context for subsidiary windows. The factory callable is user-supplied but its signature is fixed by Chevron.\n\n---\n\n**The one thing I want to confirm before writing:**\n\nYou mentioned the `WindowEnvelope` might be a type the user inherits from if they want to extend it \u2014 we discussed that and landed on the type-keyed attachment mechanism as the preferred extensibility model instead of inheritance, specifically to avoid polymorphic complexity and keep Chevron in full control of the envelope's structure. I want to confirm that's still the settled position \u2014 `WindowEnvelope` is not intended to be a user-inheritable base type, and the attachment container is the sanctioned extensibility surface.\n\nIf that's confirmed, I think we have everything we need to write a strong document with appropriately deferred sections for the PWI specifics. Does this compilation match your understanding, and is there anything here you'd push back on or add?",
2723:    "text": " These are exactly the right questions to be asking before writing anything. Let me work through each one carefully.\n\n---\n\n**On whether user code constructs the envelope directly or Chevron intervenes:**\n\nI think Chevron should intervene, and I don't think it's over-imposing at all. In fact it's consistent with the philosophy the library has maintained throughout. The factory callable the user provides should construct the raw backend window \u2014 the `wxFrame`, the `QMainWindow`, whatever the framework requires \u2014 and hand that to a Chevron-provided construction function rather than constructing the `WindowEnvelope` directly. That function takes the backend window handle and the `WindowInitContext`, assembles the envelope, populates the base attachments unconditionally, and returns the completed `unique_ptr<WindowEnvelope>`.\n\nThe user never calls `new WindowEnvelope(...)` themselves. They call something like `chevron::make_window_envelope(myFrame, context)` inside their factory body. This gives Chevron full control over the initialization sequence \u2014 base attachments are always populated in the right order, nothing can be skipped or done incorrectly \u2014 while still giving user code the freedom to construct their backend window however they need to. It also means the `WindowEnvelope` constructor can be kept private or protected, with the factory function as a friend or static factory method. The signature of the user's callable stays fixed: accept a `WindowInitContext`, return a `unique_ptr<WindowEnvelope>`. What happens inside is their domain, but the envelope itself is always Chevron's.\n\n---\n\n**On lightweight windows and deferring PWI:**\n\nThis is a genuinely good design concern and worth taking seriously. Not every window needs a full memory arena, a viewport system, and a logging context. A transient dialog or a splash screen probably shouldn't carry that overhead. A descriptor flag for this is a clean solution \u2014 something like a lightweight flag that signals to the envelope construction pathway that only the absolute minimum Chevron infrastructure should be initialized. What \"minimum\" means precisely is a deferred PWI question, but the mechanism for requesting it is settled: it lives on the `WindowFactory` descriptor alongside the existing flags, and the `WindowInitContext` assembled at dispatch time reflects that intent. The envelope then knows at construction time what tier of infrastructure to populate.\n\n---\n\n**On the name for the attachment container type:**\n\nThis type needs a name that communicates what it is without over-promising what it does. It's a container of typed per-window components. A few candidates worth considering:\n\n`WindowAttachments` \u2014 direct and descriptive, makes it clear this is the collection of things attached to a window. Slightly generic.\n\n`PWIContainer` \u2014 explicit about its purpose in the PWI context but the abbreviation may be opaque to new readers.\n\n`WindowComponentStore` \u2014 communicates the store/registry nature clearly.\n\n`WindowServices` \u2014 implies these are accessible services scoped to the window, which is close to the intended use.\n\nMy instinct is `WindowAttachments` for now \u2014 it's honest about what it is without implying anything about what's in it. But I'd like your gut reaction on that before we commit.\n\n---\n\n**On how the type-keyed attachment system actually works:**\n\nThe core mechanism is a map from type identity to stored value. In C++ the natural implementation is a `std::unordered_map` keyed on `std::type_index`, which is derived from `std::type_info` and is hashable and comparable. Each value in the map is a type-erased container \u2014 likely `std::any` or a `unique_ptr<void>` with a custom deleter \u2014 that holds the actual attachment instance.\n\nThe retrieval interface looks conceptually like this: you call `get<T>()` on the attachment container and it looks up `std::type_index(typeid(T))` in the map, retrieves the stored value, casts it back to `T`, and returns a pointer or reference. If no attachment of that type exists, it returns null or throws depending on which variant of the API you call. The storage side \u2014 `add<T>(...)` or `emplace<T>(...)` \u2014 constructs the attachment in place and registers it under its type index.\n\nWhat makes this work for PWI specifically is that each piece of Chevron infrastructure that qualifies as a base attachment is its own distinct named type. A memory arena is `chevron::WindowArena` or similar. A logging context is `chevron::WindowLogger`. Each one is retrievable by its type alone. User attachments follow the same pattern \u2014 they define a type, register it, retrieve it by type. There's no shared base class required, no virtual dispatch through the container itself. The container is just a typed registry.\n\nThe important constraint is that each type can only be registered once per envelope \u2014 a second registration of the same type is an error caught at registration time. This keeps the semantics clean: the container is not a multimap, each slot is unique per type.\n\n---\n\n**The thing I want us to think through together:**\n\nThe timing of user attachment registration. Base attachments are registered during envelope construction, driven by `WindowInitContext`. But when does user code get to register their own attachments? There are two reasonable moments:\n\nInside the factory callable itself, after `make_window_envelope` returns \u2014 the factory has a completed envelope in hand and could register attachments before returning it. This is simple and explicit.\n\nThrough a separate registration mechanism on `GUIEngine` that declares \"windows of factory X always get attachment Y\" \u2014 a pre-declared per-factory attachment list that gets applied at construction time alongside the base attachments.\n\nThe first approach is more flexible but puts the burden on the factory author to always remember to register their attachments. The second approach is more declarative and consistent with how we've handled factory registration generally, but introduces another registration surface.\n\nMy instinct is that the first approach is the right starting point \u2014 it's simpler, it keeps all the window-specific setup in one place, and it doesn't require designing another registration mechanism right now. The second approach is a natural evolution once patterns emerge in practice.\n\nWhat's your feeling on that? And what's your reaction to `WindowAttachments` as the container name?",
2753:    "text": " These are all the right concerns and there's a lot to work through here. Let me take them in order.\n\n---\n\n**On how the factory call split actually works and what user code touches:**\n\nYou're right that user code now touches `WindowInitContext` directly inside the factory body. The picture looks roughly like this: Chevron calls the factory, passing in a fully assembled `WindowInitContext`. The user's factory body uses that context to construct their backend window \u2014 the `wxFrame`, `QMainWindow`, etc. \u2014 and then hands both the backend window instance and the context to Chevron's `make_window_envelope` function. Chevron takes those two things, constructs the envelope internally, populates the base components, and returns the completed `unique_ptr<WindowEnvelope>` which the factory returns.\n\nSo `WindowInitContext` serves two purposes inside the factory call. First it provides whatever the backend window construction needs \u2014 parent handle for subsidiary windows, potentially display parameters, window title hints, or other initialization data that varies per dispatch. Second it is the authority token that Chevron's `make_window_envelope` requires \u2014 without a valid `WindowInitContext` you cannot produce an envelope at all. This is what prevents user code from constructing envelopes arbitrarily outside of a legitimate dispatch.\n\n---\n\n**On framework-specific initialization differences:**\n\nThis is a real concern but I think the ceiling you've described \u2014 wxWidgets, Qt, imgui in that order \u2014 actually helps us reason about it clearly. All three have different opinions about what a window constructor needs. wxWidgets wants a parent window pointer, a title, a position, a size. Qt is similar. imgui doesn't have persistent window objects in the same sense at all.\n\nThe way `WindowInitContext` accounts for this without becoming a framework-specific type is that it provides the framework-agnostic things Chevron knows about \u2014 parent handle if this is a subsidiary window, the instance ID being assigned, the component initialization token \u2014 and the user's factory code handles everything framework-specific directly, since they already know which framework they're using. The `WindowInitContext` doesn't need to carry a title or a size because that's the user's domain. It carries only what Chevron is responsible for injecting.\n\nThe parent handle is the interesting edge case because it comes from Chevron's own registry \u2014 specifically from the parent envelope's backend window handle \u2014 and user code can't get it any other way. That's the one framework-specific detail `WindowInitContext` needs to surface. How it surfaces it is the nuance: it probably exposes a raw `void*` or a typed accessor per supported backend so the factory can retrieve it in framework-appropriate form. That's a deferred implementation detail but the concept is clean.\n\n---\n\n**On runtime component addition and whether that's a real constraint:**\n\nYou've identified a genuine tradeoff and you're correct to question it. A pure type-keyed map populated at construction time does imply that the component set is fixed after envelope creation. That's not inherently wrong \u2014 most per-window infrastructure is naturally construction-time material \u2014 but it does close a door that might matter later.\n\nThe honest answer is that runtime component addition is possible with this mechanism, it just needs to be explicitly permitted. The `WindowComponentStore` can expose both a construction-time population pathway and a runtime registration pathway. The distinction would be that base components are always populated at construction and cannot be replaced, while optional components \u2014 both Chevron-provided and user-defined \u2014 can be added at any point during the window's lifetime as long as the envelope is alive. The type uniqueness constraint still holds \u2014 you can add a component of type T at any time, but only once. That gives you runtime extensibility without sacrificing the safety guarantee that you never have two conflicting instances of the same component type.\n\nSo the tradeoff isn't construction-time-only versus runtime \u2014 it's more precisely: base components are immutable after construction, optional components can be added at any point. That feels like the right balance.\n\n---\n\n**On `WindowComponentStore` and calling the units \"window components\":**\n\n`WindowComponentStore` is a strong name and I agree it avoids the terminology collision you flagged. Calling the individual units window components is consistent and clear. It also sets up a natural vocabulary \u2014 you register a window component, you retrieve a window component, the store holds all components for this window. That's a clean conceptual layer with its own identity.\n\n---\n\n**On how the envelope aids Chevron's central control upstream:**\n\nThis is worth articulating clearly because it's the answer to \"why does this exist.\" The envelope is the unit of currency in Chevron's window layer. Every operation that `WindowCoordinator` performs \u2014 tracking, querying, teardown ordering \u2014 is performed on envelopes. Every operation that `GUIEngine` orchestrates \u2014 subsidiary window parenting, shutdown sequencing, lifecycle event propagation \u2014 is performed through envelopes. The envelope is what gives upstream classes a uniform handle to a window regardless of what framework is underneath.\n\nMore concretely: because every live window is represented by an envelope, and every envelope is in the coordinator's registry, Chevron always has a complete and accurate picture of the application's window state. It can iterate all live windows, query the components on any specific window, wind down windows in a controlled order, propagate signals to all windows simultaneously. Without the envelope as a uniform abstraction, each of those operations would require reaching into framework-specific structures directly \u2014 which would break the layering model entirely.\n\nThe component store extends this further: because Chevron-defined base components are always present on every envelope, upstream infrastructure can reach into any window's component store and reliably find the things it needs \u2014 the logging context, the memory arena, the viewport system \u2014 without knowing anything about the specific window or its factory. That's the mechanism by which PWI becomes a first-class library feature rather than something each user has to wire up themselves.\n\n---\n\n**On whether an envelope without components is truly constructed:**\n\nThis is a sharp question. My position is that an envelope without its base components is not in a valid state, and Chevron should enforce that. Since Chevron controls the construction pathway through `make_window_envelope`, it can guarantee base components are always populated before the envelope is returned. The user cannot receive an incompletely initialized envelope from a legitimate factory call.\n\nFor user-defined components the situation is different \u2014 these are optional by nature, so an envelope without them is perfectly valid. The user registers what they need when they need it. The lightweight descriptor flag we discussed handles the case where even some base components should be skipped for genuinely minimal windows.\n\nThe factory author forgetting to register their custom components is a valid concern, but it's their concern rather than Chevron's \u2014 the envelope is correctly constructed, it just doesn't have their optional components yet. Documentation and good defaults handle that gap better than enforcement would.\n\n---\n\n**Where I think we still have open questions worth flagging for the document:**\n\nThe precise contents of the base component set \u2014 what Chevron unconditionally populates \u2014 is still deferred to the PWI design phase. The mechanism by which `WindowInitContext` surfaces framework-specific parent handles is deferred. The runtime component addition pathway exists conceptually but its API shape is deferred. The lightweight flag's precise effect on base component population is deferred.\n\nEverything else feels solid enough to write. Do you feel we've closed enough gaps to proceed to the document, or are there threads here you want to pull further first?",

Let me share my honest impressions.\n\n---\n\n**The Core Idea is Sharp and Well-Motivated**\n\nThe philosophical positioning of Chevron is one of the clearest things about it \u2014 and that clarity is a real asset. The distinction between *\"GUI application infrastructure\"* and *\"GUI framework abstraction\"* is a meaningful one that a lot of projects blur or fail to articulate. Frameworks like Qt or wxWidgets try to own everything: the widgets, the layout, the event system, *and* the application lifecycle. Chevron deliberately carves out and owns only the latter, which is a defensible and useful niche. The note in the docs clarifying that \"not concerned with widgets/layout\" does not mean \"not concerned with dynamic view mechanics\" shows you've already anticipated a very easy misread of the library's intent, which is good thinking.\n\n**The Runtime Backend Selection Decision is Interesting but Load-Bearing**\n\nThis one stood out to me. Runtime GUI framework selection is an unusual choice \u2014 most comparable infrastructure libraries either target a single backend or do compile-time selection. Runtime selection puts real pressure on how Chevron's internal abstractions are structured, since you can't lean on template specializations or compile-time dispatch to handle backend differences. It means your internal abstraction layer has to be properly polymorphic, which adds overhead and complexity. That's fine, but it will be a recurring design constraint you'll bump into, especially around the mainloop ownership problem. Speaking of which...\n\n**Mainloop Ownership is the Hardest Problem Here**\n\nThe FAQ addresses it, and the answer is the right one \u2014 Chevron must own the mainloop, full stop. But this is going to be the thorniest implementation challenge in the whole project. Frameworks like Qt and wxWidgets are *deeply* opinionated about mainloop ownership and make it genuinely difficult to invert. The \"wrapper\" approach you describe is the only real path, but it's going to look different enough per-backend that your `process/guifw/` directory is probably going to hold some of the most complex and platform-sensitive code in the library. Worth keeping that in mind as a complexity hotspot early.\n\n**The Directory Structure Tells a Story**\n\nA few observations just from reading the layout:\n\nThe separation of `include/chevron/` from `lib/include/` is interesting. `lib/` containing `suede/` suggests you have at least one internal sub-library already in mind \u2014 I'd be curious what `suede` is. Similarly, the `3rdparty/` list includes some recognizable things (Qt, wxWidgets, imgui, googletest, benchmark) alongside names I don't immediately recognize \u2014 `MsgxQ`, `xfs`, `xov`, `yarn`, `simplydt`. Those are likely either your own libraries or less common ones, and understanding what they bring to the table would probably matter a lot for discussing Chevron's internals.\n\nThe `view/` and `window/` subsystems already have meaningful internal structure (controller, navigation, page, viewport for views; apparatus, dispatch, controller for windows), which tells me you've done real design thinking on those subsystems already.\n\nThe `wx/NA/` directory under `include/chevron/wx/` is a placeholder that raises a question \u2014 is that a future wxWidgets-specific surface area, or something else?\n\n---\n\n**One Thing I Want to Make Sure I Understand Correctly**\n\nThe FAQ says Chevron does *not* take over `main()`, and that it gives the user better control rather than removing control. But Chevron also non-negotiably owns the mainloop. Those aren't contradictory, but the handshake between user-written `main()` and Chevron's mainloop ownership is an important design surface. The user has to explicitly hand off to Chevron at some point. How that handoff looks \u2014 how ergonomic and how constrained it is \u2014 will probably define a lot of first impressions of the library.\n\n---\n\nOverall, the concept is coherent and the scope is well-bounded for what it is. The main risks I see are in the mainloop ownership complexity and the runtime-selection architecture being more demanding than it initially appears. Both are solvable, just worth going in with eyes open.\n\nWhat aspect did you want to dig into first?", 649: "text": " Sure. Let me walk through what we have so far as a cohesive system, including the fringe pieces.\n\n---\n\n**AppProcess**\n\nThis is the outermost layer. It owns the process lifetime and nothing else. It holds exactly one `GUIEngine` instance, drives it through initialization and shutdown, and enforces that the sequencing rules are never violated. It doesn't know what framework is running, doesn't know what windows exist, and doesn't participate in anything GUI-specific. Its entire job is: *is the application in a valid state, and whose turn is it to act*.\n\n---\n\n**GUIEngine (abstract)**\n\nThis is the contract between `AppProcess` and every concrete backend implementation. `AppProcess` talks exclusively through this interface. The interface expresses exactly three things: initialize, run the mainloop, and shut down. Everything else is the concrete implementation's concern. `wx::Engine`, `qt::Engine`, `imgui::Engine` etc. inherit from this and provide the backend-specific behavior behind it.\n\n---\n\n**Concrete Engine implementations (wx::Engine, qt::Engine, etc.)**\n\nThese are where the actual framework coupling lives. Each one knows how to stand up its framework, wrap its mainloop so Chevron controls it, and tear it down cleanly. They own the framework's application object \u2014 the `wxApp`, the `QApplication`, whatever imgui needs at startup. They also own `WindowDispatcher` and `WindowCoordinator`, whose lifetimes are bounded by the engine's own lifetime. The user constructs one of these, configures it, and hands it to `AppProcess`.\n\n---\n\n**WindowDispatcher**\n\nLives inside the concrete engine. Responsible for the act of creating windows \u2014 it holds and executes window factory logic that results in newly constructed window instances. It sits between \"a window has been requested\" and \"a window now exists.\" It doesn't manage the lifetime of what it produces \u2014 that's not its job.\n\n---\n\n**WindowCoordinator**\n\nAlso lives inside the concrete engine. Receives what `WindowDispatcher` produces and takes ownership of those instances. Tracks what windows are alive, manages their relationships if there's a hierarchy, handles focus concerns, and knows when the last window has closed which may in turn signal shutdown. It's the ledger of the GUI layer.\n\n---\n\n**The window type itself (unnamed for now)**\n\nWhatever form it takes \u2014 whether it's `ChevronWindow` or something else \u2014 it represents a single window's lifetime and sits inside the `WindowCoordinator`. It only exists while the GUI engine is active. The layering rule is firm here: no window instance should be able to outlive the engine that owns it.\n\n---\n\n**How they interact as a system**\n\nThe flow reads cleanly top to bottom. `AppProcess` tells `GUIEngine` to initialize. The engine stands up the framework and prepares `WindowDispatcher` and `WindowCoordinator` for use. `AppProcess` then tells `GUIEngine` to start \u2014 the dispatcher materializes windows, the coordinator begins tracking them, and the mainloop runs. When shutdown comes, the coordinator winds down its windows, the dispatcher is done, the framework tears down, and control returns to `AppProcess` which completes the exit.\n\n---\n\n**Where I think the structure is solid:**\n\nThe separation between `AppProcess` and `GUIEngine` is clean and well-motivated. The `WindowDispatcher` / `WindowCoordinator` split also makes sense as a separation of concerns \u2014 creation versus management are genuinely different responsibilities and conflating them would make both messier.\n\n**Where I'd flag a potential tension:**\n\nThe relationship between `WindowDispatcher` and `WindowCoordinator` is going to need a clear handoff protocol. Specifically: when does ownership transfer from dispatcher to coordinator, and what's the mechanism? That's not a problem to solve today, but it's the first question that will surface when we design those two classes. Worth keeping in the back of your mind.\n\nThe other thing worth noting is that `GUIEngine`'s concrete implementations are going to be doing a fair amount of work \u2014 owning both `WindowDispatcher` and `WindowCoordinator`, wrapping the mainloop, managing the framework object. That's not necessarily wrong, but it means the concrete engine classes will be non-trivial. The seam between\n 48\tthose two classes is where a newly constructed window envelope transfers\n 49\tfrom one authority to the other. Neither class reaches into the other's\n 50\tdomain.\n 51\t\n 52\t# What Problem WindowDispatcher Is Solving\n 53\t\n 54\tWithout a centralized creation authority, GUI applications tend to\n 55\taccumulate the same set of problems:\n 56\t\n 57\t- Windows are created ad-hoc from arbitrary locations in user code\n 58\t\n 59\t- No clear policy exists around when a window may or may not be\n 60\t created\n 61\t\n 62\t- Business logic becomes tightly coupled to GUI construction details\n 63\t\n 64\t- There is no clean way to re-create a window that has been closed\n 65\t\n 66\t- Startup window logic cannot be reused for windows opened later at\n 67\t runtime\n 68\t\n 69\tWindowDispatcher eliminates all of these by making window creation a\n 70\tgoverned, centralized act. The exact mechanism for that cooperation is\n 122\ta deferred design question.\n 123\t\n 124\t# What WindowDispatcher Deliberately Does Not Own\n 125\t\n 126\t*This boundary is just as important as what it does own.*\n 127\t\n 128\tWindowDispatcher does not own:\n 129\t\n 130\t- The lifetime of any window it creates\n 131\t\n 132\t- Knowledge of what windows are currently alive\n 133\t\n 134\t- Focus, z-order, or any other live window state\n 135\t\n 136\t- Shutdown logic or teardown sequencing\n 137\t\n 138\t- Any GUI-framework-specific construction details\n 139\t\n 140\tOnce a window envelope leaves WindowDispatcher and enters\n 141\tWindowCoordinator, the dispatcher has no further knowledge of or\n 142\tauthority over it.\n 143\t\n 144\t# Lifetime of WindowDispatcher\n 145\t\n 146\tWindowDispatcher is constructed as part of GUIEngine at the base class\n 147\tlevel and is destroyed during GUI teardown. Construction and Registration\n 165\t\n 166\tConstructed as part of GUIEngine during the engine's own construction.\n 167\tNo GUI framework calls have occurred. The\n 196\tdispatcher handles each request uniformly: consult the descriptor,\n 197\tverify constraints, execute the factory if permitted, hand off the\n 198\tresult.\n 199\t\n 200\tFor factories carrying the single-instance flag, the dispatcher consults\n 201\tWindowCoordinator to determine whether a live instance already exists\n 202\tbefore proceeding. It is not the framework window itself \u2014 it wraps the raw backend window handle and surrounds it with Chevron's own per-window infrastructure. Its lifetime is governed entirely by `WindowCoordinator`. It only exists while the GUI engine is active.\n\n---\n\n**What the envelope carries \u2014 settled:**\n\nThe raw backend window handle \u2014 the `wxFrame*`, `QMainWindow*`, or equivalent. This is set at construction and does not change.\n\nThe typed attachment container \u2014 a type-keyed map that holds both Chevron's unconditional base attachments and any optional user-defined attachments. This is the PWI mechanism.\n\n---\n\n**What the envelope carries \u2014 the attachment model:**\n\nChevron populates a set of base attachments unconditionally at construction time for every envelope. These are the things that make sense for essentially all windows \u2014 a memory arena scoped to window lifetime, some form of dynamic view/viewport mechanism, logging context tagged to this window, lifecycle hook bindings, and whatever else the PWI design eventually prescribes. The precise list is deferred but the pattern is settled: they go in as typed attachments through the same mechanism user code uses, they're just always there.\n\nUser code can add their own typed attachments through a defined registration pathway. The retrieval interface is type-keyed \u2014 you ask the envelope for the attachment of type T and get it or get nothing. No string keys, no integers, just types as identities. Attachments don't share a common base type.\n\nThe envelope controls what can be attached and when. Chevron's base attachments are populated during construction via `WindowInitContext`. The user attachment registration pathway is a deferred design question \u2014 we know it needs to exist, we don't know its exact shape yet.\n\n---\n\n**What the envelope does not own:**\n\nWindow state visible to the framework \u2014 focus, z-order, visibility. The framework owns that. Relationship data \u2014 no parent or child references live on the envelope. That's `WindowHierarchy`'s concern. The factory accepts a single `WindowInitContext` and returns a `std::unique_ptr`. The `WindowInitContext` carries everything needed to bootstrap Chevron's base attachments unconditionally, plus optional parent context for subsidiary windows. Let me work through each one carefully.\n\n---\n\n**On whether user code constructs the envelope directly or Chevron intervenes:**\n\nI think Chevron should intervene, and I don't think it's over-imposing at all. In fact it's consistent with the philosophy the library has maintained throughout. The factory callable the user provides should construct the raw backend window \u2014 the `wxFrame`, the `QMainWindow`, whatever the framework requires \u2014 and hand that to a Chevron-provided construction function rather than constructing the `WindowEnvelope` directly. That function takes the backend window handle and the `WindowInitContext`, assembles the envelope, populates the base attachments unconditionally, and returns the completed `unique_ptr`.\n\nThe user never calls `new WindowEnvelope(...)` themselves. They call something like `chevron::make_window_envelope(myFrame, context)` inside their factory body. This gives Chevron full control over the initialization sequence \u2014 base attachments are always populated in the right order, nothing can be skipped or done incorrectly \u2014 while still giving user code the freedom to construct their backend window however they need to. It also means the `WindowEnvelope` constructor can be kept private or protected, with the factory function as a friend or static factory method. The signature of the user's callable stays fixed: accept a `WindowInitContext`, return a `unique_ptr`. What happens inside is their domain, but the envelope itself is always Chevron's.\n\n---\n\n**On lightweight windows and deferring PWI:**\n\nThis is a genuinely good design concern and worth taking seriously. Not every window needs a full memory arena, a viewport system, and a logging context. A transient dialog or a splash screen probably shouldn't carry that overhead. A descriptor flag for this is a clean solution \u2014 something like a lightweight flag that signals to the envelope construction pathway that only the absolute minimum Chevron infrastructure should be initialized. What \"minimum\" means precisely is a deferred PWI question, but the mechanism for requesting it is settled: it lives on the `WindowFactory` descriptor alongside the existing flags, and the `WindowInitContext` assembled at dispatch time reflects that intent. The envelope then knows at construction time what tier of infrastructure to populate.\n\n---\n\n**On the name for the attachment container type:**\n\nThis type needs a name that communicates what it is without over-promising what it does. It's a container of typed per-window components. A few candidates worth considering:\n\n`WindowAttachments` \u2014 direct and descriptive, makes it clear this is the collection of things attached to a window. Slightly generic.\n\n`PWIContainer` \u2014 explicit about its purpose in the PWI context but the abbreviation may be opaque to new readers.\n\n`WindowComponentStore` \u2014 communicates the store/registry nature clearly.\n\n`WindowServices` \u2014 implies these are accessible services scoped to the window, which is close to the intended use.\n\nMy instinct is `WindowAttachments` for now \u2014 it's honest about what it is without implying anything about what's in it. But I'd like your gut reaction on that before we commit.\n\n---\n\n**On how the type-keyed attachment system actually works:**\n\nThe core mechanism is a map from type identity to stored value. In C++ the natural implementation is a `std::unordered_map` keyed on `std::type_index`, which is derived from `std::type_info` and is hashable and comparable. Each value in the map is a type-erased container \u2014 likely `std::any` or a `unique_ptr` with a custom deleter \u2014 that holds the actual attachment instance.\n\nThe retrieval interface looks conceptually like this: you call `get()` on the attachment container and it looks up `std::type_index(typeid(T))` in the map, retrieves the stored value, casts it back to `T`, and returns a pointer or reference. If no attachment of that type exists, it returns null or throws depending on which variant of the API you call. The storage side \u2014 `add(...)` or `emplace(...)` \u2014 constructs the attachment in place and registers it under its type index.\n\nWhat makes this work for PWI specifically is that each piece of Chevron infrastructure that qualifies as a base attachment is its own distinct named type. User attachments follow the same pattern \u2014 they define a type, register it, retrieve it by type. There's no shared base class required, no virtual dispatch through the container itself. The container is just a typed registry.\n\nThe important constraint is that each type can only be registered once per envelope \u2014 a second registration of the same type is an error caught at registration time. This keeps the semantics clean: the container is not a multimap, each slot is unique per type.\n\n---\n\n**The thing I want us to think through together:**\n\nThe timing of user attachment registration. Base attachments are registered during envelope construction, driven by `WindowInitContext`. But when does user code get to register their own attachments? There are two reasonable moments:\n\nInside the factory callable itself, after `make_window_envelope` returns \u2014 the factory has a completed envelope in hand and could register attachments before returning it. This is simple and explicit.\n\nThrough a separate registration mechanism on `GUIEngine` that declares \"windows of factory X always get attachment Y\" \u2014 a pre-declared per-factory attachment list that gets applied at construction time alongside the base attachments.\n\nThe first approach is more flexible but puts the burden on the factory author to always remember to register their attachments. The second approach is more declarative and consistent with how we've handled factory registration generally, but introduces another registration surface.\n\nMy instinct is that the first approach is the right starting point \u2014 it's simpler, it keeps all the window-specific setup in one place, and it doesn't require designing another registration mechanism right now. GUIEngine is the class that performs that taming.\n 75\t\n 76\t# Core Responsibilities (Non-Negotiable)\n 77\t\n 78\tGUIEngine has exactly three responsibilities:\n 79\t\n 80\t1. Own and control the GUI framework environment\n 81\t\n 82\t2. Own all GUI-scoped infrastructure for the duration of GUI lifetime\n 83\t\n 84\t3. Neither reaches into\n 142\tthe other's domain.\n 143\t\n 144\t# Lifetime of GUIEngine\n 145\t\n 146\tGUIEngine is constructed by the user as a concrete implementation,\n 147\tconfigured, and then committed to AppProcess. It\n 8\tis the single point through which all window construction requests must\n 9\tpass, and it answers one question at the moment of each request:\n 10\t\n 11\t> *Is this window allowed to exist right now, and if so --- create it.*\n 12\t\n 13\tIt is not a manager, a tracker, or a policy brain. Once a window has\n 14\tbeen created and handed off, WindowDispatcher is done with it. Its\n 15\tconcern is the act of creation, not the consequences.\n 16\t\n 17\tIt is not:\n 18\t\n 19\t- A window manager or lifetime owner of windows\n 20\t\n 21\t- A GUI abstraction layer\n 22\t\n 23\t- An event router\n 24\t\n 25\t- *A one-time startup mechanism --- it remains an active, callable\n 26\t service for the entire duration of GUI lifetime*\n 27\t\n 28\t# Where WindowDispatcher Sits in the Layering Model\n 29\t\n 30\tWindowDispatcher is a GUI-scoped component that lives inside GUIEngine\n 31\tat the base class level. It is not reimplemented by each concrete\n 32\tbackend --- it is framework-agnostic infrastructure that every backend\n 33\tinherits.\n 34\t\n 35\t> Process lifetime -\\> AppProcess\n 36\t>\n 37\t> GUI lifetime -\\> GUIEngine\n 38\t>\n 39\t> \\|- WindowDispatcher (creation authority)\n 40\t>\n 41\t> \\|- WindowCoordinator (lifetime authority)\n 42\t>\n 43\t> Window lifetime -\\> \\[WindowEnvelope, TBD\\]\n 44\t\n 45\tThe division of responsibility between WindowDispatcher and\n 46\tWindowCoordinator is deliberate and non-negotiable: WindowDispatcher\n 47\tcreates windows, WindowCoordinator owns them afterward. The seam between\n 48\tthose two classes is where a newly constructed window envelope transfers\n 49\tfrom one authority to the other. Neither class reaches into the other's\n 50\tdomain.\n 51\t\n 52\t# What Problem WindowDispatcher Is Solving\n 53\t\n 54\tWithout a centralized creation authority, GUI applications tend to\n 55\taccumulate the same set of problems:\n 56\t\n 57\t- Windows are created ad-hoc from arbitrary locations in user code\n 58\t\n 59\t- No clear policy exists around when a window may or may not be\n 60\t created\n 61\t\n 62\t- Business logic becomes tightly coupled to GUI construction details\n 63\t\n 64\t- There is no clean way to re-create a window that has been closed\n 65\t\n 66\t- Startup window logic cannot be reused for windows opened later at\n 67\t runtime\n 68\t\n 69\tWindowDispatcher eliminates all of these by making window creation a\n 70\tgoverned, centralized act. User code declares window intent by\n 71\tregistering factories. The dispatcher is the only thing that ever\n 72\texecutes those factories, and only when the conditions are right.\n 73\t\n 74\t# Core Responsibilities (Non-Negotiable)\n 75\t\n 76\tWindowDispatcher has exactly four responsibilities:\n 77\t\n 78\t1. Accept window factory registrations as declarative intent\n 79\t\n 80\t2. Store and manage WindowInitContext instances that pair each factory\n 81\t with its descriptor\n 82\t\n 83\t3. Materialize windows on demand by executing the appropriate factory\n 84\t at the right moment\n 85\t\n 86\t4. Hand off newly created window envelopes to WindowCoordinator and\n 87\t relinquish all further involvement\n 88\t\n 89\tThat fourth responsibility is as important as any of the others. The\n 90\tmoment WindowDispatcher begins tracking focus, z-order, or the state of\n 91\tlive windows, it has become a manager --- which it must never be.\n 92\t\n 93\t# WindowInitContext\n 94\t\n 95\tWindowDispatcher does not store raw factory callables. It stores\n 96\tWindowInitContext instances --- lightweight objects that bundle two\n 97\tthings together:\n 98\t\n 99\t- **A window factory** --- the callable that constructs the window\n 100\t envelope when invoked\n 101\t\n 102\t- **A window descriptor** --- a flags-based metadata object that\n 103\t governs the dispatch rules for this factory\n 104\t\n 105\tThe descriptor is what allows the dispatcher to make informed decisions\n 106\tat dispatch time without containing any hardcoded policy. Flags\n 107\tcurrently envisioned include a **single-instance flag** (this factory\n 108\tmay not be dispatched if a live instance already exists) and a **main\n 109\twindow flag** (this factory produces the application's primary window).\n 110\t\n 111\tWhen the main window flag is set, the dispatcher uses that factory to\n 112\tmaterialize the first window at runtime start. If no factory carries the\n 113\tflag, the first registered factory is used by default. The main window\n 114\tdesignation also carries behavioral weight at shutdown: most GUI\n 115\tframeworks will automatically initiate application exit when the main\n 116\twindow closes, and Chevron respects that behavior rather than fighting\n 117\tit.\n 118\t\n 119\tEnforcement of the single-instance constraint requires cooperation with\n 120\tWindowCoordinator, since only the coordinator has visibility into what\n 121\twindows are currently alive. The exact mechanism for that cooperation is\n 122\ta deferred design question.\n 123\t\n 124\t# What WindowDispatcher Deliberately Does Not Own\n 125\t\n 126\t*This boundary is just as important as what it does own.*\n 127\t\n 128\tWindowDispatcher does not own:\n 129\t\n 130\t- The lifetime of any window it creates\n 131\t\n 132\t- Knowledge of what windows are currently alive\n 133\t\n 134\t- Focus, z-order, or any other live window state\n 135\t\n 136\t- Shutdown logic or teardown sequencing\n 137\t\n 138\t- Any GUI-framework-specific construction details\n 139\t\n 140\tOnce a window envelope leaves WindowDispatcher and enters\n 141\tWindowCoordinator, the dispatcher has no further knowledge of or\n 142\tauthority over it.\n 143\t\n 144\t# Lifetime of WindowDispatcher\n 145\t\n 146\tWindowDispatcher is constructed as part of GUIEngine at the base class\n 147\tlevel and is destroyed during GUI teardown. Its lifetime is entirely\n 148\tbounded by the GUI engine that owns it.\n 149\t\n 150\t> *The dispatcher exists before windows, during window creation, and\n 151\t> after windows --- but windows only exist during one slice of its\n 152\t> lifetime.*\n 153\t\n 154\tThat asymmetry is intentional. The dispatcher is not defined by the\n 155\twindows it has created. It is defined by its readiness to create them.\n 156\t\n 157\t# Lifecycle of WindowDispatcher\n 158\t\n 159\tThe dispatcher moves through three distinct operational phases. Each\n 160\tphase has different rules about what is and is not legal. An internal\n 161\tphase state governs these transitions and makes the rules enforceable\n 162\trather than merely documented.\n 163\t\n 164\t## 1. Construction and Registration\n 165\t\n 166\tConstructed as part of GUIEngine during the engine's own construction.\n 167\tNo GUI framework calls have occurred. The dispatcher is ready to accept\n 168\tWindowInitContext registrations.\n 169\t\n 170\tFactory registration is a pre-commitment activity. User code declares\n 171\twindow intent by registering factories against the engine before\n 172\tcommitting it to AppProcess. At commitment, the process-level\n 173\tregistration window closes and the factory set is effectively locked.\n 174\tPost-commitment registration from within the GUI layer is an\n 175\tintentionally deferred capability and is not part of the current design.\n 176\t\n 177\t*Factories registered here are declarative intent, not execution. No\n 178\twindows are created yet.*\n 179\t\n 180\t## 2. Runtime Activation\n 181\t\n 182\tWhen AppProcess calls startRuntime(), the dispatcher transitions to its\n 183\tactive phase. This is the first moment at which dispatch requests are\n 184\tlegal.\n 185\t\n 186\tThe dispatcher immediately materializes the startup window --- either\n 187\tthe factory carrying the main window flag, or the first registered\n 188\tfactory if no flag is set --- and hands the resulting envelope to\n 189\tWindowCoordinator. ---

**What `MemoryCore` actually is at its foundation:**

`MemoryCore` is the OS boundary. Its primary job is to acquire large contiguous blocks of memory from the OS — via `malloc`, `mmap`, or platform equivalents — hold them, and then sub-allocate from them on behalf of whoever requests budget. It does this rarely, which is exactly what you want. The cost of an OS allocation is paid once, amortized across everything that lives within that block.

The mental model is a slab allocator at the top level. `MemoryCore` acquires slabs from the OS. Everything downstream carves regions out of those slabs. The OS never sees the downstream carving — it only sees the top-level slab acquisitions, which are infrequent.

---

**The internal structure of `MemoryCore`:**

At its core, `MemoryCore` needs three things:

A collection of slabs — raw memory blocks acquired from the OS. Each slab has a size, a base pointer, and a record of how much of it has been committed to downstream consumers. When a new `MemoryScope` requests a region, `MemoryCore` finds space in an existing slab or acquires a new one.

A free list or region tracker — when a `MemoryScope` is destroyed and returns its region, `MemoryCore` needs to reclaim that space. The simplest approach is a free list of returned regions. Coalescing adjacent free regions back into larger ones is a refinement but not strictly necessary at first.

A budget ceiling — the maximum total memory `MemoryCore` is permitted to hold from the OS at once. This is the process-wide memory budget. If a request would exceed this ceiling, `MemoryCore` refuses. This is the mechanism that keeps the entire application honest about memory usage.

---

**On the slab size question:**

This is worth thinking about. If `MemoryCore` acquires slabs that are too small, it makes frequent OS calls. If they're too large, it wastes address space. A reasonable default is something like 64MB or 128MB per slab — large enough that you rarely need more than a handful of slabs for a typical GUI application, small enough that you're not reserving half a gigabyte on startup. This should be configurable at construction time.

---

**What `MemoryCore` exposes to `MemoryScope`:**

The interface between them needs to be clean and minimal. A `MemoryScope` needs to be able to do exactly two things through this interface: acquire a region of N bytes, and release a previously acquired region. That's it. The interface shouldn't expose slab internals, free list mechanics, or anything else. The `MemoryScope` receives a pointer and a size, and later hands them back.

This is where the question of whether to use an abstract interface or a template becomes relevant. Since `MemoryCore` and `MemoryScope` need to back each other through the same request mechanism, a clean abstract interface or concept constraint makes sense here. A `MemoryScope` backed by a `MemoryCore` calls `acquire(N)` on the core. A `MemoryScope` backed by another `MemoryScope` calls `acquire(N)` on that scope. The signature is identical. This is the uniformity that makes the recursive design work.

---

**What this implies about a new class or interface:**

Here's where I think an additional type may be warranted. The shared contract between `MemoryCore` and `MemoryScope` — the acquire/release interface — could be an abstract base or a C++20 concept. Let's call it the `MemoryProvider` concept for now. Both `MemoryCore` and `MemoryScope` satisfy this concept. A `MemoryScope` is templated on its backing provider type, constrained to `MemoryProvider`. This gives you zero-cost abstraction on the hot path — no virtual dispatch — while keeping the recursive backing design clean and enforceable.

This is probably not a user-facing class in its own right. It's more of a concept constraint that lives in a header. Whether it warrants its own dedicated class description document is debatable — it might just be documented as part of the `MemoryScope` description as a constraint on its template parameter.

---

**What `MemoryCore` does NOT do:**

It doesn't manage individual allocations within the regions it hands out. That's `MemoryScope`'s job. `MemoryCore` deals in large regions — hundreds of kilobytes or megabytes. The fine-grained allocation mechanics, the bump pointer, the small object optimization, all of that lives inside `MemoryScope` because that's where the actual allocation patterns of each scope's consumers are best understood.

---

Does that picture of the top-side mechanics make sense? The key architectural decision to confirm before we go further is whether you want the `MemoryProvider` concept to be an explicit named type in the codebase, or whether it's just an implicit constraint that both classes happen to satisfy. That affects whether we end up with two class description documents or three.
