But this one is actually not as scary as it sounds \\u2014 let me walk through it.\\n\\n---\\n\\n**The good news first:**\\n\\nwxWidgets, Qt, and Dear ImGui all have RTTI enabled by default in their standard builds, and none of them require you to disable it on your side. So in the typical case \\u2014 you link against a standard build of any of these frameworks \\u2014 there's no conflict. Chevron's RTTI dependency and the framework's RTTI dependency coexist peacefully because they're both compiled with RTTI on.\\n\\n---\\n\\n**Where it gets interesting:**\\n\\nQt is the one worth flagging specifically. Qt has its own parallel type system \\u2014 the Meta-Object system, `QMetaObject`, signals and slots \\u2014 which is built on top of its own code generation tool `moc` rather than standard RTTI. Qt actually works fine with `-fno-rtti` in many configurations because its own reflection machinery doesn't depend on `std::type_info`. Some Qt-heavy shops disable RTTI specifically because they feel Qt's system supersedes it. If a Chevron user is in that camp and tries to use Qt as their backend, they'd hit a conflict \\u2014 Qt's backend works without RTTI, but `WindowComponentStore` needs it.\\n\\nwxWidgets and imgui don't have this concern. wxWidgets uses standard RTTI in some of its own internals, so it essentially requires it anyway. imgui has no type system of its own and is indifferent.\\n\\n---\\n\\n**The ABI compatibility angle:**\\n\\nThe deeper concern with RTTI and mixed dependencies isn't just \\\"is it enabled\\\" but \\\"is it enabled consistently across all translation units that share types.\\\" If Chevron is compiled with RTTI on and a user links against a framework compiled with RTTI off \\u2014 or vice versa \\u2014 and they pass polymorphic types across that boundary, you can get silent undefined behavior. `type_info` comparisons across RTTI-mismatched boundaries can produce incorrect results because the type identity guarantees break down.\\n\\nIn practice for Chevron this is constrained because `WindowComponentStore`'s type-keyed operations don't cross the framework boundary \\u2014 they operate on Chevron's own types internally. The raw backend window handle crosses the boundary, but that's a plain pointer with no RTTI involvement. So the actual exposure is narrower than it might seem.\\n\\n---\\n\\n**The practical position for Chevron:**\\n\\nDocument RTTI as a requirement. State clearly that Chevron requires RTTI to be enabled and that all linked components must be compiled with RTTI on. This is a standard requirement for any library using `std::type_index` or `std::any` and won't surprise anyone building a typical GUI application. The only users who would run into trouble are those explicitly disabling RTTI, and that's an unusual enough configuration that it's reasonable to call it unsupported rather than designing around it.\\n\\nThe one thing worth keeping in mind as the library matures is that if you ever need to cross a shared library boundary \\u2014 shipping Chevron as a DLL or `.so` rather than a static library \\u2014 `std::type_info` equality across shared library boundaries has historically been fragile on some platforms, particularly older Linux configurations. My point in all of this is that if it doesn't really make since to have runtime capabilities in '`WindowComponentStore`' for PWI components, then we can simplify the design of that class in a way that steps off the RTTI ledge.\",\n6984:    \"text\": \" You've just talked yourself into the right place and I want to affirm the reasoning before we work through the solution.\\n\\n---\\n\\n**On whether runtime component addition is actually necessary:**\\n\\nThink about what PWI components actually are. They're a memory arena scoped to the window's lifetime. A logging context. A viewport system. An event bridge. These are all things that need to exist from the moment the window exists and need to be cleaned up when the window dies. There's no scenario where you'd want a window to exist for a while without a memory arena and then acquire one later. The base components are unconditional and construction-time by definition.\\n\\nUser-defined components are the only case where \\\"added later\\\" even has an argument \\u2014 but even there, think about when you'd actually add one. You'd add it when setting up the window after creation, which in practice means immediately after dispatch. You're not genuinely adding it at an arbitrary runtime moment \\u2014 you're adding it during an initialization window that's effectively still construction time from a design perspective.\\n\\nSo yes, the runtime addition capability was probably premature generalization. The honest design is: all components \\u2014 base and user-defined \\u2014 are registered at construction time or shortly after during a defined setup phase. That removes the need for thread-safe late addition entirely, which removes the mutex, which removes the `std::any` type erasure, which removes the `std::type_index` dependency, which steps off the RTTI ledge completely.\\n\\n---\\n\\n**On the shared library boundary problem more broadly:**\\n\\nEven if we kept `std::type_index`, the shared library problem is real. `std::type_info::operator==` compares by pointer on some implementations \\u2014 meaning the same type compiled into two different translation units or shared libraries can produce different `type_info` objects that compare as unequal. Your component lookups would silently fail across shared library boundaries. This is not a theoretical concern, it's a documented known issue particularly on Linux with GCC.\\n\\nThe clean escape from all of this is to not use `typeid` at all.\\n\\n---\\n\\n**The replacement mechanism:**\\n\\nInstead of `std::type_index` as the key, each component type gets a statically assigned unique ID. The pattern is simple \\u2014 a static function on each component type that returns a stable integer ID, generated once at program startup via a static local variable:\\n\\n```cpp\\nstatic ComponentID getID() {\\n    static ComponentID id = ComponentRegistry::nextID();\\n    return id;\\n}\\n```\\n\\n`ComponentID` is just an integer typedef. `ComponentRegistry::nextID()` is a simple atomic counter. No `typeid`, no `type_info`, no RTTI dependency, no shared library boundary fragility. The ID is stable for the lifetime of the process, consistent across all translation units and shared libraries because it's generated at runtime through a single counter, and the lookup is just an integer map operation.\\n\\nThe cost is that every component type must expose this static `getID()` method \\u2014 meaning user-defined components need to follow a pattern. That's a minor imposition but it's explicit and understandable, and you can make it clean with a base class or a macro or a concept constraint.\\n\\n---\\n\\n**On user code accessing envelope capabilities from within the window:**\\n\\nYou identified the right approach \\u2014 pass a reference to the envelope into the underlying window at construction time through `WindowInitContext`. The envelope has no knowledge of the window type so there's no circular dependency. The window holds a reference to its envelope and can reach its components through a well-defined interface on the envelope. User code doesn't need to know about `WindowComponentStore` directly \\u2014 the envelope exposes accessor methods that hide the storage mechanism entirely.\\n\\nWhether you want user code to hold a direct envelope reference or go through a narrower interface is a design choice. A narrower interface \\u2014 something like a `WindowContext` that exposes only what the window's internal logic needs \\u2014 would be cleaner than handing the full envelope in, because it limits what the window can do with it. But that's a refinement for when the envelope's surface is more fully designed.\\n\\n---\\n\\n**Summary of what this changes for `WindowComponentStore`:**\\n\\nDrop runtime addition. Drop the mutex. This is structural information, not a runtime state. A top-level window is a regular window. A subsidiary window was dispatched with a declared parent and its backend window was constructed with that parent relationship made real through the framework.\\n    80\\t\\n    81\\t## WindowComponentStore\\n    82\\t\\n    83\\tThe envelope owns a WindowComponentStore \\u2014 a component container that holds all per-window infrastructure associated with this window instance. Each component is a distinct named type. Components are stored under std::type_index keys and retrieved by type, with no shared base class required.\\n    84\\t\\n    85\\tChevron populates a set of **base components** unconditionally at construction time for every envelope. These are the pieces of per-window infrastructure that Chevron provides as a matter of course \\u2014 things like a memory arena scoped to window lifetime, a logging context tagged to this window, a component messaging client, and dynamic view infrastructure. It bundles the raw backend window handle produced by a user-supplied factory with the identity, lifecycle machinery, and per-window infrastructure that Chevron provides unconditionally for every window it governs.\\\\n\\\\nIt is not the framework window itself. Every instance is produced by WindowDispatcher via a factory call and immediately transferred to WindowCoordinator, which owns it for the remainder of its lifetime. The envelope exists only while the GUI engine is active.\\\\n\\\\nProcess lifetime   ->   AppProcess\\\\n\\\\nGUI lifetime       ->   GUIEngine\\\\n\\\\n                          |- WindowDispatcher    (creation authority)\\\\n\\\\n                          |- WindowCoordinator   (lifetime authority)\\\\n\\\\n                          |    |- WindowHierarchy (relationship graph)\\\\n\\\\nWindow lifetime    ->   WindowEnvelope\\\\n\\\\n                          |- WindowComponentStore (PWI components)\\\\n\\\\nThe envelope is the unit of currency in Chevron\\\\u2019s window layer. Every operation that WindowCoordinator performs \\\\u2014 tracking, querying, teardown ordering \\\\u2014 is performed on envelopes. Every operation that GUIEngine orchestrates \\\\u2014 subsidiary window parenting, shutdown sequencing, lifecycle event propagation \\\\u2014 is performed through envelopes. The uniform handle the envelope provides is what allows upstream classes to reason about any window without knowing anything about the underlying framework.\\\\n\\\\n# What Problem WindowEnvelope Is Solving\\\\n\\\\nWithout a uniform per-window container, Chevron has no clean way to associate its own infrastructure with a live window. Good — I have the full picture from the transcript. Here's the complete summary of what we decided:

---

**The original plan — `std::type_index` — and why we abandoned it:**

We started with `std::type_index` keyed on `typeid(T)` as the retrieval mechanism. The lookup would call `get<MyComponent>()`, compute `std::type_index(typeid(MyComponent))`, and find it in the map. Clean and simple.

The problem that killed it was the **shared library boundary**. `std::type_info::operator==` compares by pointer on some implementations — meaning the same type compiled into two different shared libraries can produce different `type_info` objects that compare as unequal. Your component lookups would silently fail across `.so` / `.dll` boundaries. Since Chevron explicitly supports both static and shared build configurations, this was a real problem, not a theoretical one. It's a known issue particularly on Linux with GCC.

This forced us to also reconsider whether `std::any` (which uses `typeid` internally) was appropriate. It wasn't.

---

**The settled replacement — stable static integer IDs:**

Each component type gets a statically assigned unique integer ID. The pattern is a static function on each component type:

```cpp
static ComponentID getID() {
    static ComponentID id = ComponentRegistry::nextID();
    return id;
}
```

`ComponentID` is just an integer typedef. `ComponentRegistry::nextID()` is a simple atomic counter. The ID is generated once at first call, stable for the process lifetime, consistent across all translation units and shared libraries because it goes through one counter, and the lookup is just an integer map key. No `typeid`, no `type_info`, no RTTI dependency, no boundary fragility.

The cost: every component type — both Chevron's base components and user-defined ones — must expose this `getID()` method. User code has to follow the pattern. That's a minor imposition but it's explicit and can be enforced with a base class, a macro, or a concept.

---

**The runtime addition question — and why we dropped it:**

We also decided that construction-time-only component registration is the honest design. Base components need to exist from the moment the window exists by definition. User-defined components in practice are added immediately after dispatch during a setup phase — that's effectively still construction time. There's no real scenario where you'd want a window to exist for a while and then gain a memory arena later.

Dropping runtime addition means: no mutex, no `std::any`, no `std::type_index`, no RTTI. A simpler, faster, more honest design.

---

**`WindowContext` as the user-facing proxy:**

Rather than handing user code a reference to `WindowEnvelope` directly — which would give them full access to Chevron's internal machinery — a `WindowContext` proxy is assembled by Chevron at dispatch time and delivered via `WindowInitContext`. User code can accept it in their window constructor or via a setter before returning the envelope. It exposes only the per-window capabilities the window legitimately needs: logging context, memory arena, viewport/view infrastructure. It does not expose: instance ID, factory ID, coordinator access, dispatcher access, or anything administrative.

`WindowContext` was chosen over `EnvelopeProxy` because it describes what it is from the user's perspective rather than leaking Chevron's internal vocabulary.

chat_messages.text:
You're right to push back, and I want to be honest about where that line came from.

We did discuss post-commitment registration as a deferred capability — it's listed as an open question in the `WindowDispatcher` and `WindowingSubsystem` documents. The reason it was deferred wasn't that we decided against it philosophically. It was that the mechanism for safely providing access to the dispatcher from within the running GUI layer hadn't been designed yet. The capability was acknowledged as legitimate and intentionally left for later.

So I was wrong to present it as a closed door. It isn't. The constraint we established was:

**Pre-commitment registration is always available and the factory set is locked at commitment for that registration path.** That's the bootstrapping path and it's clean and simple.

**Post-commitment registration — runtime factory addition — is a real capability that was deferred pending the design of the access mechanism**, not rejected.

---

**Why there's nothing semantically preventing it:**

You're correct. The dispatcher already knows how to accept a factory and assign it an ID. There's nothing about that operation that requires the mainloop to be stopped or the engine to be in a pre-committed state. The only real question is thread safety — if the dispatcher's factory storage is being written to at runtime while dispatch calls could be reading from it concurrently, that access pattern needs to be safe. But that's a solvable engineering problem, not a fundamental design objection.

The mechanism we hadn't designed was specifically how user code inside the running application reaches the dispatcher to register a new factory. The natural answer, given what we now know, is through `WindowContext` — the same surface through which runtime dispatch requests flow. If `WindowContext` exposes a `registerFactory()` path alongside `dispatch()`, then runtime registration becomes available to any running window that holds a `WindowContext`.

---

So to directly answer your question: no, you're not mistaken, and yes, it makes sense. Runtime factory registration is a legitimate capability. We deferred the mechanism, not the idea. Should we factor that into the conceptual snippet for the factory callable, or work through it as part of the window interior perspective later?

Instead, Chevron provides a controlled construction function that is the only legitimate way to produce an envelope instance.\\\\n\\\\nInside a factory callable, the flow is:\\\\n\\\\n- The user code factory call receives a WindowInitContext assembled by Chevron at dispatch time\\\\n\\\\n- The factory constructs the backend window instance using information from the WindowInitContext as needed \\\\u2014 including the parent window handle for subsidiary windows\\\\n\\\\n- The factory passes the backend window handle and the WindowInitContext to the Chevron defined envelope constructor method\\\\n\\\\n- Chevron constructs the envelope internally, assigns identity, populates base components, and returns a std::unique_ptr<WindowEnvelope>\\\\n\\\\n- The user code factory returns that pointer, transferring ownership to WindowDispatcher, which immediately hands it to WindowCoordinator\\\\n\\\\nThis pathway ensures that no WindowEnvelope can exist without a valid WindowInitContext having been involved in its construction. The WindowInitContext is the authority token that makes the construction legitimate. Without it, there is no envelope.\\\\n\\\\n# What WindowEnvelope Deliberately Does Not Own\\\\n\\\\n*This boundary is just as important as what it does own.*\\\\n\\\\nWindowEnvelope does not own:\\\\n\\\\n- Window state visible to the framework.\\\\n\\\\n- Relationship data.\\\\n\\\\n- Its own lifetime \\\\u2014 that belongs to WindowCoordinator.\\\\n\\\\n- Knowledge of other live envelopes or the state of the application\\\\u2019s window population.\\\\n\\\\n- Any framework-specific API surface beyond holding the raw handle.\\\\n\\\\n# Lifetime of WindowEnvelope\\\\n\\\\nAn envelope is born when WindowDispatcher fires a factory and transfers the result to WindowCoordinator. It lives for as long as WindowCoordinator holds it in its registry. It is destroyed when the coordinator winds it down, either as part of the shutdown sequence or in response to the underlying framework window being closed.\\\\n\\\\nDuring teardown, the envelope\\\\u2019s components are destroyed in the reverse order of their registration. The backend window handle is released last. At the end of teardown, the envelope is removed from the coordinator\\\\u2019s registry and destroyed. Nothing may reference it after that point.\\\\n\\\\n*An envelope\\\\u2019s lifetime is the window\\\\u2019s lifetime from Chevron\\\\u2019s perspective. When the envelope is gone, the window is gone.*\\\\n\\\\n# Error Handling Philosophy\\\\n\\\\nWindowEnvelope and its construction pathway should:\\\\n\\\\n- Treat any attempt to construct an envelope outside of Chevron\\\\u2019s control as a hard error\\\\n\\\\n- Guarantee that base components are fully populated before the envelope is returned from construction\\\\n\\\\n- Catch duplicate component registrations immediately and surface them as errors\\\\n\\\\n- Fail fast on any attempt to access the component store after the envelope has begun teardown\\\\n\\\\n**Note: **The boundary between returned error codes and thrown exceptions follows the same open question as the rest of the library \\\\u2014 deferred pending library-wide error handling strategy decisions.\\\\n\\\\n# Open Questions and Deferred Decisions\\\\n\\\\nThe following are known open questions that are intentionally deferred:\\\\n\\\\n- **Base component set: **The precise set of components Chevron populates unconditionally in every envelope \\\\u2014 which subsystems qualify, what they are named, and in what order they are initialized \\\\u2014 is deferred to dedicated PWI design work.  5\\t# What WindowInitContext Is\\n     6\\t\\n     7\\tWindowInitContext is the **dispatch-time initialization token** that Chevron assembles and passes into a factory callable at the moment a window is created. It is Chevron\\u2019s side of the factory contract \\u2014 the structured object that authorizes and parameterizes the construction of a WindowEnvelope.\\n     8\\t\\n     9\\tIt exists for the duration of exactly one factory invocation. It is not constructed by user code, not stored after the factory returns, and not reused across dispatch calls. Its lifetime is the factory call itself.\\n    10\\t\\n    11\\tIt serves two distinct audiences within that single invocation: Chevron\\u2019s own envelope construction function, which consumes the internal bootstrapping data it carries, and the user\\u2019s factory body, which may query it for dispatch-time information needed to construct the backend window correctly.\\n    12\\t\\n    13\\tIt is not:\\n    14\\t\\n    15\\t- A configuration object the user builds or customizes\\n    16\\t\\n    17\\t- A service locator or general-purpose context object\\n    18\\t\\n    19\\t- Reusable or storable beyond the factory call it was assembled for\\n    20\\t\\n    21\\t- A channel for passing user-defined construction parameters\\n    22\\t\\n    23\\t# Where WindowInitContext Sits in the Layering Model\\n    24\\t\\n    25\\tWindowInitContext does not occupy a persistent position in the runtime hierarchy. It is a transient object that materializes at the dispatch boundary \\u2014 the seam between WindowDispatcher firing a factory and WindowEnvelope coming into existence \\u2014 and disappears once that boundary has been crossed.\\n    26\\t\\n    27\\tProcess lifetime   ->   AppProcess\\n    28\\t\\n    29\\tGUI lifetime       ->   GUIEngine\\n    30\\t\\n    31\\t                          |- WindowDispatcher    (creation authority)\\n    32\\t\\n    33\\t                          |    |- [WindowInitContext lives here, transiently]\\n    34\\t\\n    35\\t                          |- WindowCoordinator   (lifetime authority)\\n    36\\t\\n    37\\tWindow lifetime    ->   WindowEnvelope\\n    38\\t\\n    39\\tGUIEngine assembles it, the dispatcher passes it into the factory call, the factory uses it to construct the backend window and hand everything to Chevron\\u2019s envelope construction function, and then it is gone. No class in the system holds a reference to it after the factory returns.\\n    40\\t\\n    41\\t# What Problem WindowInitContext Is Solving\\n    42\\t\\n    43\\tThe factory callable has a fixed signature: it accepts a WindowInitContext and returns a std::unique_ptr<WindowEnvelope>. This constraint exists because Chevron needs to guarantee that every envelope is constructed through a controlled pathway, one where the internal identity, component bootstrapping, and structural metadata are always correctly initialized.\\n    44\\t\\n    45\\tWithout WindowInitContext, there is no mechanism to enforce that guarantee. A factory that constructs a WindowEnvelope without Chevron\\u2019s involvement could produce an envelope with no instance ID, no base components, and no valid place in the coordinator\\u2019s registry. The context is the token that makes construction legitimate \\u2014 it cannot be forged by user code, and without it Chevron\\u2019s envelope construction function will not proceed.\\n    46\\t\\n    47\\tAt the same time, the context gives the factory body access to the one piece of Chevron-managed information that user code genuinely cannot obtain any other way: the parent window handle for subsidiary windows. That handle lives inside another live envelope in WindowCoordinator\\u2019s registry. The context is the bridge that carries it out to where it is needed.\\n    48\\t\\n    49\\t# Core Responsibilities (Non-Negotiable)\\n    50\\t\\n    51\\tWindowInitContext has exactly two responsibilities:\\n    52\\t\\n    53\\t- Carry Chevron\\u2019s internal dispatch-time data into the envelope construction function, authorizing and parameterizing the construction of a valid WindowEnvelope\\n    54\\t\\n    55\\t- Expose dispatch-time information to the factory body that user code needs to construct the backend window correctly\\n    56\\t\\n    57\\t*WindowInitContext is a transient token, not a service. It carries information in one direction \\u2014 from Chevron into the factory \\u2014 and is consumed once.*\\n    58\\t\\n    59\\t# What WindowInitContext Carries\\n    60\\t\\n    61\\t## Chevron-Internal Data\\n    62\\t\\n    63\\tThe internal contents of WindowInitContext are consumed exclusively by Chevron\\u2019s envelope construction function. User code has no reason to interact with them and they are not part of the public-facing API of the context. The public API will include at minimum the dispatch identity information: the ID of the factory being dispatched, the window instance ID, and the WindowKind for this dispatch. The internal bootstrapping tokens the WindowComponentStore initialization requires are not publicly accessible. The precise internal contents are deferred to the PWI design phase.\\n    64\\t\\n    65\\t## The Parent Window Handle\\n    66\\t\\n    67\\tFor subsidiary window dispatches, the context carries the parent window handle retrieved by GUIEngine from the parent envelope\\u2019s backend window reference. This is the one piece of information the factory body may need that it cannot obtain from any other source.\\n    68\\t\\n    69\\tThe handle is surfaced through a typed accessor \\u2014 getParentAs<T>() \\u2014 where T is the framework-specific window type the factory expects. Since the factory author already knows which GUI framework is in use, the cast is safe and the correct type is always known at the call site. Chevron stores the handle internally as a void* and the accessor performs the cast, keeping the context itself framework-agnostic while giving the factory body a clean, type-safe retrieval path.\\n    70\\t\\n    71\\tFor regular top-level window dispatches, the parent handle slot is absent. Querying it in that context is a misuse and must be caught. The WindowKind carried by the context gives the factory body a clean way to branch on this if needed.\\n    72\\t\\n    73\\t# User-Defined Construction Parameters\\n    74\\t\\n    75\\tWindowInitContext deliberately does not provide a mechanism for passing user-defined construction parameters into the factory. That is not its responsibility. The factory callable itself is the correct vehicle for that.\\n    76\\t\\n    77\\tBecause the factory is any callable with the correct signature \\u2014 not just a plain function \\u2014 it can close over whatever context it needs. A lambda captures local variables from the registration site. A functor class holds member state and exposes operator() with the required signature. Either approach gives the factory body access to application-specific construction data \\u2014 settings objects, database handles, configuration structs, whatever the window requires \\u2014 without Chevron needing to know anything about it.\\n    78\\t\\n    79\\tThis is not a workaround. It is the intended model. The factory is a closure and closures carry their own context. Chevron provides WindowInitContext for the things only Chevron can provide. Everything else is the factory author\\u2019s domain.\\n    80\\t\\n    81\\t# Lifetime and Ownership\\n    82\\t\\n    83\\tWindowInitContext is assembled by GUIEngine at dispatch time, passed into the factory callable, and consumed by Chevron\\u2019s envelope construction function before the factory returns. It does not outlive the factory call.\\n    84\\t\\n    85\\tTo enforce this, WindowInitContext is non-copyable and its constructor is not accessible to user code. It cannot be stored, forwarded, or reused. A factory that attempts to retain a reference to the context beyond the scope of its invocation is producing undefined behavior.\\n    86\\t\\n    87\\t*WindowInitContext exists for the duration of one factory call. It **is created** **for** the dispatch** request**, **then destroyed** **after** the envelope** exists**. Nothing holds it after that.*\\n    88\\t\\n    89\\t# What WindowInitContext Deliberately Does Not Own\\n    90\\t\\n    91\\t*This boundary is just as important as what it does carry.*\\n    92\\t\\n    93\\tWindowInitContext does not own:\\n    94\\t\\n    95\\t- Any WindowEnvelope instance\\n    96\\t\\n    97\\t- Any user-defined construction parameters\\n    98\\t\\n    99\\t- Any reference to the parent envelope or the coordinator\\u2019s registry\\n   100\\t\\n   101\\t- Knowledge of what happens after the factory returns\\n   102\\t\\n   103\\t- Any state that persists between dispatch calls\\n   104\\t\\n   105\\t# Error Handling Philosophy\\n   106\\t\\n   107\\tWindowInitContext and the dispatch pathway around it should:\\n   108\\t\\n   109\\t- Refuse construction of a WindowEnvelope if the context was not legitimately assembled by Chevron at dispatch time\\n   110\\t\\n   111\\t- Catch any attempt to query the parent handle on a context assembled for a top-level window dispatch\\n   112\\t\\n   113\\t- Treat any attempt to construct or copy a WindowInitContext outside of the dispatch pathway as a hard error\\n   114\\t\\n   115\\t**Note: **The boundary between returned error codes and thrown exceptions follows the same open question as the rest of the library \\u2014 deferred pending library-wide error handling strategy decisions.\\n   116\\t\\n   117\\t# Open Questions and Deferred Decisions\\n   118\\t\\n   119\\tThe following are known open questions that are intentionally deferred:\\n   120\\t\\n   121\\t- **Internal contents: initialization \\u2014 is deferred to dedicated PWI design work.\\n   122\\t\\n   123\\t- **Envelope construction function name and signature: **The Chevron-provided function that accepts the backend window handle and WindowInitContext to produce a WindowEnvelope exists as a defined concept but its precise name, namespace, and C++ signature have not been finalized.\\n   124\\t\\n   125\\t- **Parent handle storage type: **The void* approach for storing the parent handle internally is a workable baseline. Let me break it down clearly.\\n\\n---\\n\\n**What a hook is, fundamentally:**\\n\\nA hook is a defined point in a system's execution where external code can be attached and called automatically. The system doing the work says \\\"at this moment, I will call anyone who has registered interest in this moment.\\\" The registered code \\u2014 the hook \\u2014 runs at that exact point without the system needing to know anything specific about what it's doing.\\n\\nThe simplest mental model is a notification slot. The system owns the slot. Someone else fills it with a callable. When the system reaches that point in its execution, it calls whatever is in the slot.\\n\\n---\\n\\n**What a lifecycle hook specifically is:**\\n\\nA lifecycle hook is a hook tied to a specific moment in an object's lifetime \\u2014 creation, initialization, destruction, or notable state transitions in between. The word \\\"lifecycle\\\" just means the hook fires at a meaningful point in the object's life rather than at an arbitrary moment.\\n\\nCommon lifecycle moments that warrant hooks:\\n\\n- **On create** \\u2014 fires right after the object is fully constructed and ready\\n- **On destroy** \\u2014 fires right before the object begins teardown\\n- **On activate / on deactivate** \\u2014 fires when the object enters or leaves an active state\\n\\n---\\n\\n**How it works mechanically:**\\n\\nAt its simplest, a lifecycle hook is a stored callable \\u2014 a function pointer, a `std::function`, a lambda \\u2014 that the owning class holds as a member. At the appropriate moment in its lifecycle, the class calls it. Something like:\\n\\n```cpp\\nif (onCreateHook) onCreateHook(*this);\\n```\\n\\nMore sophisticated hook surfaces allow multiple registrations \\u2014 a list of callables rather than one \\u2014 so multiple subscribers can respond to the same lifecycle moment independently.\\n\\n---\\n\\n**Why it applies to `WindowEnvelope`:**\\n\\n`WindowEnvelope` represents a live window's lifetime from Chevron's perspective. Chevron's internal subsystems \\u2014 the logging context, the memory arena, the viewport system \\u2014 all need to know when a window comes into existence so they can initialize their per-window state, and when it goes away so they can clean up. When you call `store.add<MyComponent>(...)`, internally it does something like:\\n\\n```cpp\\nstd::type_index key = std::type_index(typeid(T));\\nmap[key] = /* stored component */;\\n```\\n\\nAnd retrieval mirrors it:\\n\\n```cpp\\nstd::type_index key = std::type_index(typeid(T));\\nauto it = map.find(key);\\n```\\n\\n---\\n\\n**Does this require RTTI?**\\n\\nYes, but with an important nuance. `typeid(T)` where `T` is a concrete, fully known type at compile time does **not** strictly require RTTI in the traditional sense. RTTI \\u2014 Runtime Type Information \\u2014 is primarily needed when you call `typeid` on a **polymorphic object through a base pointer or reference**, because that's where the runtime dispatch into the vtable is needed to determine the actual dynamic type. `typeid` on a plain concrete type like `typeid(MyComponent)` is resolved at compile time and doesn't technically need the RTTI machinery that `dynamic_cast` depends on.\\n\\nHowever, `std::type_info` and `std::type_index` are part of the RTTI infrastructure, and most compilers treat them as requiring RTTI to be enabled. In practice, if you compile with `-fno-rtti` on GCC or Clang, `typeid` becomes unavailable entirely and the code won't compile. So while the theoretical dependency is narrow, the practical dependency is: **RTTI must be enabled**.\\n\\n---\\n\\n**What this means for Chevron:**\\n\\nSince Chevron targets Linux, macOS, and Windows with GCC, Clang, and MSVC, RTTI is on by default on all three. The question is whether any downstream user of Chevron would want to disable it \\u2014 which is occasionally done in embedded or game engine contexts for binary size or performance reasons. Chevron doesn't need to know that the window has a context, it just provides the means to create one.\\n\\nDoes that flow sit right with you?\",\n7116:      \"new_str\": \"---\\n\\n## 8. `WindowComponentStore`, RTTI, and the `WindowContext` Proxy\\n\\n### The Problem That Started This\\n\\n`WindowComponentStore` was originally designed using `std::type_index` as the key for its component map, with `std::any` for type-erased storage. This approach depends on `typeid(T)`, which is part of the RTTI infrastructure. The question arose: does Chevron have an RTTI dependency, and what are the implications?\\n\\n---\\n\\n### The RTTI Dependency Chain\\n\\n`typeid(T)` on a concrete type doesn't strictly require runtime dispatch, but `std::type_info` and `std::type_index` are part of the RTTI infrastructure and most compilers make them unavailable when RTTI is disabled (`-fno-rtti`). So in practice: **if you use `std::type_index`, you depend on RTTI being enabled**.\\n\\nThis becomes a real problem \\u2014 not just a theoretical one \\u2014 when Chevron is built as a shared library (`.so` / `.dll`). `std::type_info::operator==` on some implementations compares by pointer identity rather than by name. The same type compiled into two different shared libraries can produce different `type_info` objects that compare as unequal. Component lookups across shared library boundaries would **silently fail**. Since Chevron explicitly supports both static and shared build configurations, this is not a concern for later \\u2014 it is a concern now.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### The Runtime Addition Question \\u2014 Was It Actually Necessary?\\n\\nBefore redesigning the storage mechanism, the more fundamental question was asked: **does `WindowComponentStore` actually need to support runtime component addition at all?**\\n\\nPWI components are things like memory arenas, logging contexts, viewport systems, and event bridges. These are all things that need to exist from the moment the window exists and be cleaned up when the window dies. There is no practical scenario where a window legitimately needs to exist for a while without a memory arena and then acquire one later. Even user-defined components, which at first seem like a case for runtime addition, are in practice registered during a defined setup phase immediately after dispatch \\u2014 effectively still construction-time from a design perspective.\\n\\n**Conclusion: runtime component addition was premature generalization.** The honest design is that all components \\u2014 base and user-defined \\u2014 are registered at construction time or during a defined post-construction setup phase. This removes the need for late addition entirely.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### The Causal Collapse of the RTTI Dependency\\n\\nOnce runtime addition is off the table, the requirements that drove the original design fall away one by one:\\n\\n1. ~~Runtime addition from any thread~~ \\u2192 no longer needed\\n2. ~~Mutex to guard concurrent access~~ \\u2192 no longer needed\\n3. ~~`std::any` for type-erased storage of arbitrarily-timed additions~~ \\u2192 no longer needed\\n4. ~~`std::type_index` as the map key~~ \\u2192 no longer needed\\n5. ~~RTTI dependency~~ \\u2192 no longer needed\\n\\nThe design simplifies cleanly and the shared library problem is eliminated at the root.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### The Replacement Storage Strategy\\n\\nInstead of `std::type_index`, each component type gets a **statically assigned unique integer ID** generated once at program startup via a static local variable and an atomic counter:\\n\\n```cpp\\nstatic ComponentID getID() {\\n    static ComponentID id = ComponentRegistry::nextID();\\n    return id;\\n}\\n```\\n\\n- `ComponentID` is a simple integer typedef\\n- `ComponentRegistry::nextID()` is an atomic counter \\u2014 increments once per type, once per process lifetime\\n- No `typeid`, no `type_info`, no RTTI dependency\\n- Consistent across all translation units and shared libraries \\u2014 the ID is generated at runtime through a single counter, not derived from type identity metadata\\n- Lookup is a plain integer map operation\\n\\nThe cost is that every component type \\u2014 including user-defined ones \\u2014 must expose a static `getID()` method. This is a minor but explicit imposition on user code. It can be made clean through a base class, a concept constraint, or a registration macro. The explicitness is a feature, not a bug \\u2014 it makes the contract visible.\\n\\n---\\n\\n### `WindowContext` \\u2014 The Envelope Proxy\\n\\nUser code's underlying window class (their `wxFrame` subclass, their `QMainWindow` subclass, etc.) legitimately needs access to Chevron's per-window capabilities \\u2014 logging, memory arenas, viewport systems. But handing the full `WindowEnvelope` to user code would give them unchecked access to Chevron's internal currency: coordinator registry operations, lifecycle hook manipulation, direct component store modification. That is not acceptable.\\n\\nThe solution is a **dedicated proxy type** that sits between the envelope and the underlying window class, exposing only the per-window capabilities that user code legitimately needs. This type is named **`WindowContext`**.\\n\\n`WindowContext` exposes roughly:\\n- Access to the window's logging context\\n- Access to the window's memory arena\\n- Access to the window's viewport / view infrastructure\\n- Whatever other Chevron services are scoped to this window\\n\\n`WindowContext` does **not** expose:\\n- Instance ID or factory ID\\n- `WindowCoordinator` or `WindowDispatcher` access\\n- Lifecycle hook manipulation\\n- Anything that would let user code interfere with Chevron's window tracking\\n\\n---\\n\\n### The `WindowContext` Construction Constraint\\n\\nAn important constraint emerged during design: **`WindowContext` can only be created after the `WindowEnvelope` exists**, because the proxy must reference a live envelope. This means it categorically cannot be passed into the user's window constructor through `WindowInitContext` \\u2014 the envelope doesn't exist yet at that point.\\n\\nThe correct flow inside a factory callable is:\\n\\n```\\n1. Receive WindowInitContext\\n2. Construct the backend window instance\\n3. Call Chevron's envelope creation function \\u2192 receive unique_ptr<WindowEnvelope>\\n4. Call chevron::make_window_context(*envelope) \\u2192 receive WindowContext\\n5. Pass WindowContext to the window via a setter (e.g. window.setContext(std::move(ctx)))\\n6. Return the unique_ptr<WindowEnvelope>\\n```\\n\\nChevron provides a publicly accessible `make_window_context()` function (name not yet finalized) that accepts an envelope reference and returns a `WindowContext`. Chevron controls what the proxy exposes. It exposes only the interface Chevron intends: add a page, remove a page, navigate to a page. The underlying framework's full API is deliberately constrained at this surface \\u2014 viewports are containers for pages and nothing else. User code does not subclass `Viewport`.\\n\\n**`Page`** inherits from the framework's view base (`wxPanel`, `QWidget`, etc.) and exposes the full native GUI API \\u2014 it is a view, and user code does normal framework work inside it. Instead, Chevron provides a controlled construction function that is the only legitimate way to produce an envelope instance.\\\\n\\\\nInside a factory callable, the flow is:\\\\n\\\\n- The user code factory call receives a WindowInitContext assembled by Chevron at dispatch time\\\\n\\\\n- The factory constructs the backend window instance using information from the WindowInitContext as needed \\\\u2014 including the parent window handle for subsidiary windows\\\\n\\\\n- The factory passes the backend window handle and the WindowInitContext to the Chevron defined envelope constructor method\\\\n\\\\n- Chevron constructs the envelope internally, assigns identity, populates base components, and returns a std::unique_ptr<WindowEnvelope>\\\\n\\\\n- The user code factory returns that pointer, transferring ownership to WindowDispatcher, which immediately hands it to WindowCoordinator\\\\n\\\\nThis pathway ensures that no WindowEnvelope can exist without a valid WindowInitContext having been involved in its construction. The WindowInitContext is the authority token that makes the construction legitimate. Without it, there is no envelope.\\\\n\\\\n# What WindowEnvelope Deliberately Does Not Own\\\\n\\\\n*This boundary is just as important as what it does own.*\\\\n\\\\nWindowEnvelope does not own:\\\\n\\\\n- Window state visible to the framework.\\\\n\\\\n- Relationship data.\\\\n\\\\n- Its own lifetime \\\\u2014 that belongs to WindowCoordinator.\\\\n\\\\n- Knowledge of other live envelopes or the state of the application\\\\u2019s window population.\\\\n\\\\n- Any framework-specific API surface beyond holding the raw handle.\\\\n\\\\n# Lifetime of WindowEnvelope\\\\n\\\\nAn envelope is born when WindowDispatcher fires a factory and transfers the result to WindowCoordinator. It lives for as long as WindowCoordinator holds it in its registry. It is destroyed when the coordinator winds it down, either as part of the shutdown sequence or in response to the underlying framework window being closed.\\\\n\\\\nDuring teardown, the envelope\\\\u2019s components are destroyed in the reverse order of their registration. The backend window handle is released last. At the end of teardown, the envelope is removed from the coordinator\\\\u2019s registry and destroyed. Nothing may reference it after that point.\\\\n\\\\n*An envelope\\\\u2019s lifetime is the window\\\\u2019s lifetime from Chevron\\\\u2019s perspective. When the envelope is gone, the window is gone.*\\\\n\\\\n# Error Handling Philosophy\\\\n\\\\nWindowEnvelope and its construction pathway should:\\\\n\\\\n- Treat any attempt to construct an envelope outside of Chevron\\\\u2019s control as a hard error\\\\n\\\\n- Guarantee that base components are fully populated before the envelope is returned from construction\\\\n\\\\n- Catch duplicate component registrations immediately and surface them as errors\\\\n\\\\n- Fail fast on any attempt to access the component store after the envelope has begun teardown\\\\n\\\\n**Note: **The boundary between returned error codes and thrown exceptions follows the same open question as the rest of the library \\\\u2014 deferred pending library-wide error handling strategy decisions.\\\\n\\\\n# Open Questions and Deferred Decisions\\\\n\\\\nThe following are known open questions that are intentionally deferred:\\\\n\\\\n- **Base component set: **The precise set of components Chevron populates unconditionally in every envelope \\\\u2014 which subsystems qualify, what they are named, and in what order they are initialized \\\\u2014 is deferred to dedicated PWI design work. Good, I found everything I need from the transcript. Here is the full picture of what we established:

---

**The four sanctioned injection points:**

We settled on exactly four types where Chevron inserts itself into the framework's inheritance hierarchy. These are the ceiling — the goal is to never need a fifth.

`chevron::wx::Window` — inherits from `wxFrame`, mirrors `WindowKind::TOP_LEVEL`
`chevron::wx::Subwindow` — inherits from the appropriate subsidiary base, mirrors `WindowKind::SUBSIDIARY`
`chevron::wx::Viewport` — inherits from the framework's container widget, implements the Chevron viewport contract
`chevron::wx::Page` — inherits from the framework's view base, implements the Chevron page contract

---

**The additive-only rule:**

`Window` and `Subwindow` are additive only — they introduce infrastructure helper methods and nothing else. They do not override anything, shadow anything, or interfere with the user's ability to use the full framework surface. Because inheritance is public, a `chevron::wx::Window` subclass can be passed anywhere a `wxFrame` is expected. The user loses nothing from the framework side.

What they add is things like `attachViewport()` — methods that handle registration ceremony with Chevron's infrastructure automatically. What they explicitly do not add is layout helpers, event convenience methods, or anything that abstracts or replaces framework functionality.

---

**The close notification problem:**

We identified window close notification as an open unsolved problem. The additive-only rule means Chevron cannot use method overrides to hook into framework close events — that would be overriding behavior, not adding it. The most promising direction identified was external binding via the framework's own event system — `Bind()` in wxWidgets, signals in Qt — but the precise mechanism was left as a deferred open problem.

---

**`WindowEnvelope` remains agnostic — non-negotiable:**

This was stated explicitly and firmly. The envelope holds a raw backend window handle. Whether that handle points to a raw `wxFrame` subclass the user wrote entirely themselves, or a `chevron::wx::Window` subclass, is completely irrelevant to the envelope. Nothing in the process layer makes any assumption about the window type. This property must be maintained as the library grows.

---

**These types are conveniences, not requirements:**

`Window` and `Subwindow` are optional. A user who subclasses `wxFrame` directly and registers viewports manually through `WindowContext` is using Chevron correctly. The manual `WindowContext` registration pathway must remain fully functional alongside the base types, always.

---

Good timing to revisit this — it's a pivotal type and it has a lot of responsibility concentrated in a small surface. Let me give you the full picture.

---

**What it is fundamentally:**

`WindowContext` is a proxy. It sits between `WindowEnvelope` — Chevron's internal per-window infrastructure container — and the user's window class. The user's window holds a `WindowContext` and uses it to reach Chevron's per-window capabilities. The envelope itself never touches user code directly.

The reason the proxy exists is protective. `WindowEnvelope` is Chevron's internal currency — it carries instance IDs, factory IDs, coordinator registry membership, lifecycle hook surfaces, direct component store access. Handing that to user code would give them unchecked access to Chevron's internals. `WindowContext` exposes only what a window's internal logic legitimately needs and nothing more.

---

**How it comes into existence:**

This is the constraint that shapes everything else about it. `WindowContext` can only be created after its `WindowEnvelope` exists, because the proxy must reference a live envelope. This means it categorically cannot be delivered through `WindowInitContext` into the window's constructor — the envelope doesn't exist yet at that point in the factory flow.

The correct factory flow is:

```
1. Receive WindowInitContext
2. Construct the backend window
3. Call Chevron's envelope creation function → get unique_ptr<WindowEnvelope>
4. Call chevron::make_window_context(*envelope) → get WindowContext
5. Deliver WindowContext to the window via a setter
6. Return the unique_ptr<WindowEnvelope>
```

Chevron provides `make_window_context()` — or whatever the final name settles on — as a publicly accessible factory function. Chevron controls what goes into the proxy. The envelope never surfaces to user code.

---

**What it exposes:**

`WindowContext` is a capability surface, not an administrative surface. Roughly:

- The window's logging context — scoped to this window's lifetime
- The window's memory arena — scoped to this window's lifetime
- The viewport/page navigation interface — `context_.viewport("name").navigateTo<SomePage>()`
- Runtime factory registration — the ability to register new window factories from within a running window
- Runtime window dispatch — the ability to request that a registered factory fires and produces a new window

What it deliberately does not expose: instance ID, factory ID, `WindowCoordinator` access, `WindowDispatcher` access, lifecycle hook manipulation, component store access, or anything that would let user code interfere with Chevron's window tracking machinery.

---

**Its lifetime:**

The proxy's lifetime is bounded by the window's lifetime. If the user holds a `WindowContext` and `WindowCoordinator` destroys the underlying envelope, the proxy becomes dangling. In practice this is safe because if the window object is alive, its envelope is alive — `WindowCoordinator` will not destroy an envelope while the framework window still exists. The documented contract is that the proxy's validity is bounded by the window's existence. The user is responsible for not retaining it beyond that.

---

**Why it's the convergence point for both paths:**

As you saw in the snippets, the two construction paths — `chevron::wx::Window` with `attachViewport()` and raw `wxFrame` with `context_.registerViewport()` — converge the moment construction is done. After that, both paths use `WindowContext` identically. Navigation, logging, dispatch requests, factory registration — all of it flows through the same `WindowContext` surface regardless of which base type the window used. That's not accidental — `WindowContext` is specifically designed to be the one stable interface the window's internal logic ever needs to touch. Everything Chevron provides at the per-window level is reachable through it.

---
